We have later the report, which was wholly non-committal, of Colonel Anderson, with specifications and drawings, and the unqualified commendation of Colonel Hughes. What was done next we know nothing. The minister tells us that he revised the contract, making twenty drafts of it. And then we have the contract between the Ross Rifle Company and the Crown. Before coming to this, however, there were certain tests made in Quebec. And, in this connection, I think I may say that the counsel for the Ross Rifle Company did not help his case by his conduct before the committee. I do not think that his treatment of Major Pym and General Cotton was of a kind that should have been tolerated before a committee of this House. I do not think that in reference to the tests made before the contract he was altogether fair and correct in his statements. He referred to the Ross rifle and the Lee-Enfield being subjected to a charge of 35 tons. It seems that, hy the terms that were agreed upon by the committee, there was to be such a test, but when they got to Quebec they did not make such a test. Yet Mr. Nesbitt put it that, having agreed that such tests were to be made, and the fact that men of such standing as General Otter and Major Gaudet reported in favour of the rifle, showed that they must have been made. Whereas he must have known, if he knew anything about it, that such a test was not made. The report said :
A cartridge loaded with a charge of 10 grains of cordite, calculated to produce a pres sure of 22 tons per square inch was employed. Thermo. 70 P.
1st round.-Percussion cap blown out. Action very stiff ar.d considerable force exerted by haimmeniing with heel to open breeoh.
2nd round.-Same result. Sir C. Ross declined to allow rifle to fire further excessive charges. Locking lugs examined after firing and found unaltered. Total rounds fired 1,441.
Now, I want to be perfectly fair. The Ross rifle was subjected to a test of 22 tons, but the Lee-Enfield to only 17:69 tons. But the Lee-Enfield came through the trial prefectly unharmed. So, though a great deal was made in the committee of the additional strength of the Ross rifle, it proved nothing. It was subjected to a heavier test and went to pieces, and the Lee-Enfield was subjected to a lighter test and came out all right. This does not afford a basis for a comparison favourable to the Ross rifle.
Now, the contract was made, and I suppose that this is one of the things the minister is proud of, the record of which he would wish to have engraved on his monument when he is called upon to leave this world and pass to another where war is no more. There are just a few comments

I would like to make on the contract. First, there is the reason given for the contract being made, and that reason is set out on the face of the contract. Let us see if in this there is a justification for this expense. The preamble says :
Whereas, it is considered in the general interests of Canada that the rifles required by the government for the purposes of militia and defence should be manufactured in Canada, and whereas the contractor has proposed by himself or his assigns to undertake the establishment and operation of a suitable factory in Canada for the manufacture of such rifles.
Now, are they manufactured in Canada?
I do not propose to waste time discussing that. We may bandy words across this floor, but the fact remains that there is not a man in Canada but knows exactly whether those rifles are manufactured in Canada or not. Certain words have a certain meaning. When we speak of a rifle factory in Canada, in order to have our rifles manufactured within our own borders, the ordinary man knows what that ought to mean. It must mean that we can manufacture rifles independent of any foreign power.
As we manufacture cotton, for instance.

My hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean), like the hon. Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden), apparently cannot see the difference between a rifle factory and a cotton factory. I suppose that in case of difficulty cotton would not be contraband of war, and that we should be able to bring in cotton. But we certainly could not bring in arms. The government does not establish a cotton factory as it establishes an arms factory, in order that we may be independent of other countries. How can we be independent in this manufacture even if one essential part of the rifle is manufactured outside our owrn borders? It is all very well for the minister to say that the bulk of these things made outside came in in the shape of forgings. That makes no difference ; if you cannot manufacture your rifle wholly in Canada, there is no object, from that point of view', in having it manufactured here. The hon. gentleman says that we are not supporting the navy of Great Britain because we have not control of the expenditure, but we will help the down-trodden Englishmen by making a contribution by having arms manufactured in Canada instead of England. But I think it would pass the logic of the minister to show how the down-trodden Englishman is to benefit by having arms manufactured here instead of in England.

The stock of the English rifle is imported from Italy, and, I believe, the stock of the American
rifle also. I think there are some other parts of the English rifle that are manufactured in Belgium.

I can quite understand tnat it might be advisable, if England does not raise the wood necessary, to import the stocks. But I can understand also that it would be easy enough to have a sufficient quantity of them on hand. And, as an hon. gentleman beside me suggests, wood w'ould not be contraband in time of war. But when we have only one little factory for the manufacture of rifles, it must be selfevident that the manufacture in Canada is of no value unless practically every bit of the rifle is made here-and on that subject there wras no dispute before the committee. The gentlemen examined before the committee rather fenced as to the extent to w'hich the manufacture was carried on in icanada, but it could not be denied that, up to a certain point, the parts were manufactured and brought into Canada. But there is no part of the Ross rifle that is made in Canada.

The steel
is not made in Canada.

Then, if the w'hole rifle is not manufactured in Canada, literally or substantially, what is the justification or advantage of having a factory here at all ; what is the use of it, when the factory could be put out of business in twenty-four hours?
The steel may be made here.
When these articles are made here, and with another and a w'iser government in powrer, it might be well to start a factory. But until these articles are made here-
Then the hon. gentleman w'ould have waited until every particle of steel and all the materials could be made in Canada?

I would have waited until so much of the component parts could be made in Canada that there was a reasonable certainty that tne remainder could be made in a short time. I think then the establishment of a factory would be justifiable.

And the hon. gentleman's own friends started a cartridge factory, and until this much-abused government came into power every single thing that entered into the manufacture of those cartridges was imported. To-day the shells and a great many other things, practically all are made in Canada.
Quite possibly.
I quoted the prices of the rifle from the trade. The statement the hon. gentleman has just read is not correct.

It is absolutely correct.
I have the honour to report, for your information, that I have carefully inspected the above rifle in all is details, and I find it
superior, in my opinion, in every way to the Lee-Enfield.
He had evidently been reading a lette from Col. Hughes, you see.
I consider the straight pull a decided ad vantage and the resisting power greater thai that *01 the Lee-Lii field. The magazine, bac and fore-sights are also a decided improve rnent; the pistol grip, too, an importan change; in fact the whole mechanism of th xifle is more simple in its construction fo cleaning and repairing purposes.
1 would consider this rifle might be mann factured in reasonable quantities for, say tb sum of twenty-five ($25) dollars, and wouid b a fair value. This rifle cannot be ohtainei in the English or any other market. Evei were this rifle placed in the open market to day, I am still of the opinion, in view of th< material improvements, it could not be sup plied at a less figure than above mentioned viz., $25.
It is not correct.
My authority is better than that of the minister a good deal and I challenge the minister to go to his books in his department and disprove my statement.

The hon. gentleman refused to distinguish them. I

say it is not fair to compare the price paid the Boss Rifle Company with the price charged by the War Office.
I am going right on to give the two
Not if I had not called the hon. gentleman's attention.
The average price is not fair, it is the price to the trade that must be considered.

The average price is fair for this reason :	It would be most
grossly unfair for me to say the government should get rifles from the Ross Company as cheaply as from the War Office. It is equally unfair to compare the price to the Ross Company with the price paid to the trade in England.
Oh, no.

Certainly most ridiculously unfair. If the minister will tell me of any private factory in England which the government furnishes with all the land it requires and all the working capital needed. I will admit that it is fair to compare the Ross prices with those of such a factory, but until he can do so I say it is unfair.
The only difference in England is that the War Office pays in advance the whole amount.
A letter was read this afternoon in which the trade offers to supply the rifle referred to with an advance of only 10 per cent of the amount.
That is not correct.
The letter was read and it is absolutely correct.
I have seen the letter and it is absolutely correct.
It is not [DOT]correct.
It was read and it will not do for the minister to deny everything of which he knows nothing.
I dispute that anyway.

The minister showed how much idea he had of the price of rifles when he added the duty. He says that the rifle would cost $17 and he adds to the cost the amount of the duty. He knows that would not pay the duty and that it would not add to the price if it did. We only pay the duty to ourselves, from one department to anothex-. The question is what it would cost the country one way or the other, and if it would not cost the country any duty in one case then it is preposterous to add the duty in comparing prices. The American government has a rifle which some people think is quite equal to the Ross rifle. I have here a statement, and I think the minister will understand it, which shows the cost to the American government. This is an official letter to the Secretary of State stating that the cost of a rifle to the American government is $14.90, and if it only costs the American government $14.90 to make a rifle it seems to me that we can hardly be said to have secured a rifle on as reasonable terms as the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence has claimed, because we pay Sir Charles Ross $25 and you allow all his material free entry into the country, make him a present of the land and advance him heaven knows how much money. I will come to that later on. I think I have shown that the preamble of the contract has not been carried out, that the rifles are not manufactured in Canada and that they are not as cheap as they could be got in England. Whereas in England we bought our bayonets for 11 shillings-they only cost the War Office 7s 4d-but buying them from the trade we get them for 11s., which is a shade over $2-the Americans get their bayonets for $1.49 apiece.
I thought 11s. was more than a shade over $2.
It would be under $2.25.	[DOT]
I think 11s. is nearly $3.

Taking into ^consideration the minister's price of $5.12, 60 cents on the dollar would not be considered a very great difference. We find by the correspondence of Colonel Cotton that the Ross rifle is not adapted to the bayonet.
That is not true. There is no rifle with a bayonet in England. The bayonets are made in a different place altogether-made by different people.
I am not saying that the bayonet was made in England, but the bayonet goes with the rifle in England.
If you choose to buy it.
We did buy it 'with tlie rifle.
We did not buy it from the same place.

I never stated that *we bought it in the same place. I am pointing out that the rifle and bayonet can be made so that they can go together because they do go together. The correspondence of Colonel Cotton shows that the Ross rifle is not adapted to the bayonet.
That is not correct.
That is in his correspondence and I can show that.
No, some one was stupid enough to ask if the Lee-Enfield bayonet would fit the Ross rifle.
It was not a case of Lee-Enfield at all. I will find it later.

I think the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Worthington) asked the question.
Mi\ NORTHRUP, I was speaking of the contract. Let me go a little farther n ith this contract. I have only got through the preamble. The contract provides that the government shall receive 12,000 rifles between the 1st January, 1903, and the 1st January, 1904. Then it is provided that subsequently any rifles that the government shall require shall be bought from this company. So that the contract is ah absolutely perpetual contract. The government were not bound to buy any number ot rifles from this company and that is the only defect in the contract as far as I can see from the contractor's standpoint. Every other thing that the contractor could conceive of was in the contract except that but I suppose that perhaps the minister thought that owing to the exigencies of parliamentary life he dare not put any specific quantity in the contract; so that fiom year to year the contractor would have to rely upon the goodness of the minister and have to stand in with the minister to secure the extension of his contract.

MACLEAN, essence of the contract?
What was the
Cash. I think.

I admit that was a very important part of it, but I would like to ask my hon. friend if he considers that the essential part of the contract was that the contractor was obliged to sell rifles or whether the essential part of the contract was that tlie contractor was obliged to manufacture rifles for the government.
It is not an ordinary contract of purchase and sale?
It is not an ordinary contract, I must agree ; it is the most extraordinary contract that I ever saw in my life.
Do not be funny. It was not an ordinary contract of purchase and sale?

No, nobody will claim that. To go on with this contract, it is admitted that the contract is a perpetual contract, the price being $25, but that may be raised as provided by the contract. Then there is another extraordinary clause. I wonder if this is the particular clause upon which the Minister of Militia and Defence bases his claim to bright, green recollection in the memory of his fellow countrymen after he is gone? It is as follows :
Provided, however, that in case of war, actual or threatened, or any national emergency, requiring, in the opinion of the government, the immediate supply of additional arms, the contractor, upon receiving any notice or demand from the government for any number of rifles specified to be urgently required in view of this proviso, shall, within thirty days after receiving such notice or demand, notify the government in writing of the number of rifles which he will undertake to furnish in accordance with such notice or demand, and the government shall not, under any circumstances, be bound to purchase from the contractor in respect of any such notice or demand any number of rifles in excess of the number which the contractor so notifies the government that he will be able to supply.
I think my bon. friend (Mr. A. IC. Maclean) bad that clause in his mind when he asked me if this was an ordinary contract. We might imagine the jester of a European monarch suggesting in his monarch's ear after the fifteenth course at dinner such an absolutely absurd provision as this. If war breaks out with the States and if we are short of arms the government has the right to call on the contractor to state how many rifles he can furnish and then, after he has thirty days to make up his mind about it, by which time in all probability the Americans will have swept the country, he is to tell the government how many he can supply and then the government are not bound to buy any more from him than the number he has named. No wonder the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence is proud of this monument he has erected in the hearts of his countrymen.
That is very funny.
The contractor was not obliged to manufacture rifles unless they were ordered. If the government ordered rifles he had to manufacture them Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.

It is the funniest thing I ever saw in my life. Then there is the provision that the government has to pay $25 for each rifle. But here is another

extraordinary clause. I have not the faintest idea what it means, but it is here :
The price for all rifles herein contracted for or to he supplied pursuant to the provisions of this agreement shall he payable upon delivery; provided, however, that after the establishment of the said factory and supplying of the plant for the running of the same the contractor shall be entitled to payment in advance of delivery of moneys actually expended upon the rifles or parts thereof or fixtures therefor to be delivered in that year.
You have to give the contractor every dollar he has put in, only in no ease is the payment to exceed 75 per cent of the price of such rifles. The meaning is perfectly clear. The rifle is sold for $25, the contractor is entitled to 75 per cent of $25, which is $18.25. Looking at the reasonable profits on this rifle and looking at what it costs the American government to construct its rifle and at what it costs the English government to construct its rifles, we see that $18 would more than furnish the contractor with all the working capital he requires. How was this thing really worked out? Colonel Wurtele was examined and we found out from him. 1 told the minister that I thought the examination was perfectly absurd and I stand by it. Here is what took place. The contract provides that this 25 per cent is only to be paid on the certificate of the contractor who is to satisfy the government inspector of small arms. The contract, therefore, is dependent solely on the gov. eminent inspector of small arms. The government had an inspector of small arms there, Mr. Gaudet, and Mr. Gaudet was instructed to take charge of this inspection. Mr. Gaudet was sensible enough to know that he could not discharge the duties that were imposed upon him; he knew that no man living could. When Mr. Gaudet found he was charged with the duty of examining in order to certify the 75 per cent he objected, and at page 235 of the report it will be found that Mr. Gaudet says :
After careful consideration, it is found impossible, under this system to carry out the instructions received, in guaranteeing that the percentage laid down in the contract shall not be exceeded, for the following reasons:
2. The shipments of materials received consists of barrels, receivers and sundry components, far too numerous to mention; to comply with the contract, it is necessary to know the relative value of each component to that of the finished rifle. Similarly, as regards wages, it is necessary to establish the amount which should be expended on each component, in addition to materials, to produce rifles costing not more than $25 each. If the contractor pays more for materials or w-ages than is necessary, to produce rifles costing $25, the department will be paying a higher percentage than authorized by contract, and thus the invoices or statements produced are inadequate and of little value 'r) determining the amount of advances.
It was the same way about the labour; if the labourers were idle and did not earn 100 cents on the dollar of their wages the government would be paying too much. He says:
The result of this misrepresentation is that an unauthorized advance of $8,000 on fixtures [DOT] has already been made. What has happened in the case of this special clause, will unavoidably occur again, as I am not conversant with the law relative to the interpretation of contracts, nor have I the advantage of knowing what the parties intended by the present agreement, and repetition of such mistakes may cause trouble to the department. The surest way of precluding a recurrence of such errors, is that the contracting parties, who know the exact meaning of the terms to which they agreed, should themselves furnish interpretations and instructions for the guidance of those concerned.
8. It will be clear from the foregoing that the duties and responsibilities devolving on the inspector are greater than they appear at first sight, and are perhaps in excess of what was intended by the department. Tor reasons stated above, I beg to be relieved of the responsibility of recommending advances, and that these as well as the interpretation of the contract be dealt with at Ottawa.
There was an honest intelligent man who saw he could not follow out the conditions of this contract, and therefore he asked to be relieved. The government at once took a Col. Wurtele who was at that time In the employ of the Ross Rifle Company. He was not paid by the government it is true; he owed no obligation to the government, he was simply an employee of the Ross Rifle Company and he may be a worthy and excellent man, but according to his own evidence he took the invoices simply and whatever was on their face went. He never heard of a commission for cash, he never heard of trade discounts and Inasmuch as every one in business knows, it is as certain as the Ross rifle factory is in Quebec that Sir Charles Ross would never pay cash without getting his trade discounts. We have it as plain as can be that when the government advances 75 per cent on the value of the rifles which means 100 per cent of the value of the goods up to the 75 per cent, Sir Charles Ross is getting perhaps 100 per cent more than he should get if the real truth were known as to the trade discounts he receives. In the same way when Col. Wurtele looks at the wages account he simply sees how much wages is paid and if any man is idle the government loses, and if any man does inferior work the government is losing also. You have absolutely no check in the world either on the value of the material supplied or on the value of the work done. That would be bad enough in all conscience, and that went on for years until the Auditor General had his attention called to it and perhaps it would be interesting to see what the Audi

tor General did about that. Iu the Auditor General's reports for the fiscal year ending 1907, I find an order in council, which was passed in consequence of a letter from the Auditor General addressed to the Deputy Minister of Militia, dated, Ottawa, June the Sid, 1907, which winds up in this way:
Let me call your attention to clause 8, where provision is made for the certificate of the inspector of small arms as to the amounts expended by the contractor and upon which the advances have been made, and permit me to say that, wrhile the progress estimates are certified to by the inspector he has informed me that he is not certifying of his own knowledge but on the strength of a certificate made by Mr. Ernest Wurtele, a chartered accountant at Quebec. Now, Mr. Wurtele, may be competent to make the certificate on behalf of the contractor, but as he is not. in the employ or under the control of the government his certificate cannot he accepted under the Consolidatel Revenue and Audit Act. If this arrangement of certificates has been made with the consent or on the instrutions of the department and advances made on the strength of these certificates aggregating over $800,000 I must say, that it is not only unbusiness-like but also illegal and no certificates of this nature will be knowingly accepted by this office.
And so we have over the signature of the Auditor General of Canada that under this contract the Minister of Militia deliberately went ahead, overrode the terms of the contract itself and illegally, without any justification whatever paid out over $800,000 to Sir Charles Ross on the certificate of an employee of Sir Charles Ross. Was there ever such a business transaction in this or any other country? Here is this government first agreeing to advance 100 per cent of the value of the goods, all the goods cost, up to 75 per cent of the value of the rifles, and it leaves it to an employee-I care not how honourable Col. Wurtele may be-it leaves it to an employee of Sir Charles Ross who makes out a certificate: amount of material so and so; amount of labour so and so, and the government promptly paid on that certificate to the tune of $800,000.
'Sir FREDERICK: BORDEN. The same man is doing the work now'.

Ah, yes, the same man is doing the work now, and the government is paying so much more and the same man is doing it because while your Inspector of small arms should do the work you drew your contract so stupidly that you gave that officer work that he could not do, and as a sane honest man would not attempt to do. Then, you put the duty on an employee of tlie Ross Rifle Company, and when you were held up by the Auditor General and you could not pay on his certificate, then iu order to carry on your

payment to your friends you bring that employee of the Ross Rifle Company over to the government, give him $5 a day and he does the same work as lie did before, but this time he does it at the expense of the government. And that is considered a fair business-like way of looking after the interests of the country. And since the minister has been good enough to interrupt me let me see how Mr. Wurtele came over to the government. He came over under a memorandum from the Minister of Militia to council dated the 12tli September, 1907, which, after reciting tlie circumstances, reads as follows:

Wurtele, R.O., was consequently employed for the work and that officer has certified to all progress estimates, which have been paid to the Ross Rifle Company since the contract was entered into, before such progress estimates were authorized for payment.
That is, Col. Wurtele has authorized every single payment up to date says the minister in the order in council. Is that true? The first payment that was made was made on May 2Gth, 1903, and if we look at the report of the Public Accounts Committee, page 230, we will find Mr. Gaudet was the man who certified to that.
Ross Rifle Works, Quebec, Canada. Payment application No. 1.
On account of certificate of expenses No. 1 for $91,000, I hereby apply for the payment of $25,000 on account. I hereby certify that I have produced fixtures and material with du- _ plioates of receipted hills attached hereto, for the inspection of the acting inspector of small arms.
I also certify that I have insured the said fixtures for the benefit of the government and deposited the policy with the Bank of Montreal of this city.
(Sgd.) CHARLES L. ROSS.
I hereby certify the above to he a true and accurate statement and recommend payment of the $25,000 on account.
(Sgd.) E. M. GAUDET, Major,
Acting inspector of small arms.
Quebec, March 21, 1903.
On the 25th of March, 1903, Major Gaudet sends tlie certificate to the department, and on the 26th of March, 1903, as appears by the Auditor General's Report, $25,000 was paid. So, when the order in council states as the reason for appointing Major Wurtele that be signed every progress estimate since tne contract began, I have proved from the files brought down by my bon. friend that, at all events, the first $25,000 was not paid on progress estimates, and I do not know how much more. The reason why Major Wurtele was appointed is thus stated by the order in eouucil:
That before the payment of any such progress estimate, it became apparent that this

provision of the contract could not be satisfactorily carried out because it was undesirable that such payments should be made upon the certificate of the contractor and because of the labour verifying every item thereof, which would devolve upon the inspector of small arms, would seriously interfere with his usefulness as such.
So Major Gaudet made a report showing that the reason he objected to certiry was that no honest man could do it, and therefore he asked that the authority be taken at Ottawa for ordering the money to be paid. 1 say that the order in council brought in by the Minister of Militia recites, not the fact as set out in Major Gaudet's report, but another reason altogether. Surely, if there were nothing else in this contract, this in itself would be sufficient to justify suspicion-that we find in one minute of council two statements which are utterly foreign to the facts set out in the documents brought down by the Minister of Militia himself. The contract also provided that all' tools and machinery and raw materials could be brought into this country free of duty. It also recited that any finished parts used in such rifles could be brought in free of duty, showing that at the very time the contract was made the minister understood that finished parts would be imported. It seems to me that if the minister had been anxious to have the rifles manufactured in Canada as soon as possible, and had allowed the unfinished parts to be brought in free of duty, he would have required the duty to be paid on the finished parts to encourage their production in this country.
Now, how did the contract work out ? Advances, of course, were called for by the Boss rifle jieople almost at once. We have in the Auditor General's Keport, at page Q-104, a statement showing w7hat the advances were. There is one interesting statement, however, which I would like to give the House, and which, I think, will be surprising to some of the members. I spoke of the valuation being $25. In addition to the rifles we purchase, we have to purchase a great many component or multiple parts, and my information leads me to believe that a great many of these have to be purchased. By a subsequent contract between the company and the government it is arranged that the price to be paid for the component parts added together would be $31 instead of $25, but another inspection increases that to $32. Then advances were made, and for a long time not many rifles were produced. Up to the end of the year 1905 about $600,000 had been paid and only 136 rifles had been delivered. The minister may have thought that was a business transaction, but it seems to me that it would strike the ordinary man that there was something radically wrong wTith a contract which, made in March, 1902, required 12,000 rifles to be delivered in the following year, whereas the statement brought down by the department itself shows that up to the end of 1903 $600,(XX) had been advanced and 136 rifles had been delivered.
The hon. gentleman will be glad to know that 41,200 have been delivered now.

I would be glad if I thought that the rifles were what the minister tells us they are ; but, having the reports of officers and men all over the country who have suuered from the use of these rifles, I am obliged to conclude that hie less we get of them the better off we shall be. At the end of the next year 14,-Ooo rifles had been delivered and $800,000 had been advanced.
Something was said this afternoon about the immense amount of wages that wrere pant by the Ross iune Company. 1 am not in a position to say just what wages they do pay, because I have never been in their employ ; but I find a statement, on pages 101, 106 and 126 of the last file brought down, which shows that from the 14th of December, 1906, to the 8th of March, 1907, the total Bill for superintendence and labour was $40,140; from the 8th of March, 1907. to the 16th* of August, 1907, it was $42,421; and from the 16tli of August, 1907, to the 30th of August, 1907, it was $2,521, making altogether about $85,000 paid for superintendence and labour from the 4th of December, 1906, to the 30th of August, 1907. During these eight and a half months they were supposed to be manufacturing, and I give the figures for these months, because they are the only months for which the returns seem to be brought down. I wish just briefly to recapitulate two or three * other points which will show how this contract has been carried on. Very shortly after the contract was made it became necessary to decide what to do about drawings and specifications. They had neither specifications nor drawings, and any hon. member who will take the trouble to read the blue-book will find out how pathetically Colonel Pauet kept writing to Montreal to Colonel Gaudet, begging him to see the Ross Company and have them consent to supply drawings and specifications. The pleadings of the Militia Department were most piteous, showing how7 completely it was at the mercy of the contractor. Finally they agreed upon specifications, but conditional on the minister allowing the contractor to bring in what he liked free from the United States.
Would the hon. gentleman repeat the figures lie gave for the wages last year?

On page 101 of the latest file brought down in April last, I

found the accountant's certificate to the order of 24th December, 1906, for superintendence and labour from the 15th March. It goes down from week to week from the 15th March to the 16th August, and the sum total is $42,421.32. On page 106 from 14th December to 8th March superintendence and labour $40,140.86. On page 126, from 16th August to 30th August, $4,474.18. That would be really three weeks. While this was $4,474.18 I only gave it at $3,528 because two of these weeks overlapped. At the bottom of one of these which I gave before, we find the week that comes up to the 16th August. It struck me as odd that the same week should be in the one place as $1,904 and the other as $2,258-apparently the same week.
After the difficulty about plans and specifications, there came the difficulty about gauges. The department wrote the Ross Company, as soon as they realized that difficulty, that the company must supply the gauges. Major Gaudet was of the opinion that the company should supply the gauges, but the company did not supply them, and after a time the government yielded and gave a contract to the company for these gauges. The contract price was $32,000, and that price ^vas given iu the face of the letter of Major Gaudet pointing out that, since there had been no test, he could not give any idea as to whether the price was reasonable or not. The gauges were contracted for on the 14th April, 1903, and they were to be supplied within eight months from that date and there was a clause providing as follows:
Terms-One-half in four months of the acceptance of this tender upon establishing to the satisfaction of the department that fair progress had been made in the manufacture of the gauges and furnishing certificates that the value of the material then in our possession to be used for this work, and the cost of labour in connection therewith, together amount to at least half the total cost of the gauges when completed.
It seems hardly credible, but not a single gauge turned up in the eight months. More months went on and then some material was supplied. Then apparently some 160 gauges were actually supplied. After this the rifle was changed from No. 1 to No. 2 and the gauges were of no use and so no more were got. Practically the result therefore was that the government paid for a lot of gauges which they never received, which were not even made. The total number was to be 489. Not one was supplied until months after the contract had expired. Eventually 162 were supplied. Then when the contract was put an end to, it was put an end to verbally so that it is Impossible to know the exact date, and for aught we know the company may have gone ahead manufacturing gauges after the rifles had been changed. They claimed Mr. NORTHRUP.
that they were to supply 489, they did supply 162, and said they had ready for delivery 197, yet the government never saw them. Then the company claimed that they had a number of gauges amounting to 130, for which the drawings were made and the material supplied, so that although the government only received 162 out of 489, they paid $26,000 on a $32,000 contract.
Then there was a dispute about some cocking pieces. The government as usual yielded and paid the company a couple of thousand dollars. Then there was a dispute about the sight. A new sight was asked for, the government yielded, and put up $15,000 for a sight. But perhaps the coolest thing of all was a letter from the Ross Company stating that they wanted to stow away some 9,000 rifles and asking for storage room. The government, desiring, of course, to be reasonable, said they would furnish storage room, but the cost of transportation each way would be at the expense of the company. Here is the letter which was written by Col. Cotton:
March 30, 1905.
The Ross Rifle Company made a proposition to the Militia Department to the effect that the department should lend storage room for about 9,000 incompleted rifles, Mark I, until brought forward for completion. These rifles to be transported to and from at the expense of the Ross rifle factory. To facilitate the movement of these rifles, it was decided by the minister to accept an offer of the company to make 400 boxes each to contain 10 complete rifles and to purchase such boxes at the price each of $1.50.
But after getting the minister to agree to buy 400 boxes at $1.50 each, the company came back and said the boxes at that price would not be satisfactory, but that boxes at $2 each would suit. So the minister paid $2 each for 400 boxes to transport 9,000 incompleted rifles for storage until it would be convenient for the company to complete them. That illustrates the way the business was carried on.
Let me call attention to this other fact. The government has spent enormous sums on inspection in addition to the purchase price of these rifles. It takes a great deal to have rifles inspected. You have to put up buildings, heat them, pay salaries, &c. By the time the 50,000 rifles are delivered, the government will have spent at least $150,000 for inspection alone. They have paid over $125,000 to date in connection with the inspection, in which I include the various items of salaries, heating, &c. Here are the details:
Travelling expenses	$ 1,500
Salaries of inspector's staff	 45,823
Materials for inspection	 3,390
Heating, lighting, rent,	&c.. ..	2,188
Extra parts, gauges, &c	 53,029
Total	$124,942

This is the expenditure up to last March in connection with inspection. So it will come to $150,000 by the time all the rifles are delivered, so that we must add $3 to the price of the rifles there.
Now, talking about heating and lighting, there was a rather odd occurrence in the committee. The Boss Rifle Company claimed quite a large bill for heating and lighting the premises. This was referred to Colonel Cartwright, and if you take the trouble to refer to pages 304-5 and 373 of the report, you will find in full what X will give only briefly. Sir Charles Ross said to the government, in effect : You have been occupying a part of my premises up to 1st May, 1905, and after that date, you occupied more. We have to heat the premises and we want you to make us some allowance. So he put in a claim for $1,740 up to 1st May, 1905-
I bring this matter up because it illustrates the way Colonel Cartwright did everything in Quebec in connection with the Ross Rifle Company. He seems to have figured up a certain number of cubic feet that were lying around loose, and, where the company claimed $1,746, he came to the conclusion that they were entitled to $2,247. They claimed for the period after 1st May, $2,614, and he found, by his method of calculation, that thev were entitled to $3,166. Their total claim was $5,233, but Colonel Cartwright thought that their bill should have been $6,604. And the government paid them $2,294 and they were mighty thankful to get it. And to make matters more humorous-as the minister seemed to like to look at things in that light, if you will look at the evidence of Major Gaudet before the Public Accounts Committee, you will find that he was asked when he left, and he said he was in the Ross rifle factory up to July 1, 1905. He was asked how much room the government occupied there, and his reply was that it was a little space, ' not bigger than this platform,' referring to the platform in the Public Accounts Committee. So. we have Major Gaudet, who was in charge, and must have known the facts stating that the space occupied was very small. And it must have been, because up to 1905, only 136 Ross rifles had been delivered. so that not much room could be required.
Now, there was another little matter to which I should refer in connection with the historv of this affair, and that is the test of rifles at Regina. It was rather an odd tiling, because it was done two or three months after the contract was entered into. .At PP-238. 239 and 241 will be found the record of the facts. There is a peculiar letter at page 373 to which I would call the attention of the House. This rifle whs taken up to Regina. Those who have read the report will remember what took place. Two rifles were taken there. One was taken for examination, but was blown up, and so they sent for another. It was clear that they found
fault with the rifle, but it was pointed out that ail they had done was to test it for accuracy and that they knew nothing about its endurance. They wanted a sample to be made and put into the hands of the troops, and they decided that it would not be satisfactory until tried by them. A letter appears from the Minister of Militia, of which the following is a portion :
May 16, 1904.
Dear Colonel White,-I am in receipt of a letter from Sir Charles Ross, dated 12th instant, from which I make the following extract :
In the summer of 1902, the Northwest Mounted Police made a test of my rifle at Regina, with the result that its adoption was decided upon. I inclose you a copy of the report. A pattern was then sealed, which met with their requirements.
The minister comes to the conclusion that the man must be crazy to write such a letter. The committee had not approved the rifle, there was no sealed pattern and he must be dreaming. The only explanation I can make of the examination in Regina was that it was done that some such letter might be written and some department might be induced to purchase rifles for the mounted police, because the contract was made in March and this did not take place until the following summer. And there is an odd letter from Sir Charles Ross at page 470 of the last file brought down :
Now the state of affairs I found would, if discovered by the attackers of the government, have given them unadulterated joy, and would have been a really effective weapon not only against the whole department but against the government itself.
What was the state of affairs, I wonder, that he found when ho came back?
Now, Sir, I have many points on which I would like to speak, but at this late hour I will be merciful to the House.
An bon. MEMBER. Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman need not be ' here, here,' unless he likes. Certainly, I should not if I did not have to. There was one matter that it seemed to me the government was singularly careless about, and that was particularly impressed upon me when Mr. Wallace Nesbitt was here. To my mind, nothing was plainer, in the examination by Mr. Nesbitt before the committee, than that the object was to lay the basis of a lawsuit against the government for damages in consequence of the way they had interfered with the manufacture of his rifle. The whole line of questioning, the suggestions to the witnesses, the line taken by Sir Charles Ross undoubtedly was : You agreed that I should manufacture a certain rifle, you agreed to a certain sample of a sealed pattern. The government had a sealed rifle, but they had no more than got it sealed than changes were

made. Sir Charles Ross requested the first change. If you look into the correspondence, you will see that quite plainly. He wanted a change of a sight and a change of a cocking piece and receiver. Changes were made by him and also by the government. And how did it work out practically'/ So many changes were made that Mr. Nesbitt gave us before the committee a list, which is printed here, of over eighty changes that were made. Changes were made oefore the rifle was adopted at all. Sir Charles Ross asked for the three I spoke of. Then the government made others. Then this committee, of which my bon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) is so distinguished an ornament, made fifteen changes, and when these changes were communicated to Col. Cartwright he wanted another. And the changes made in 1901 to Mark I. made Mark II. They went on and changed Mark I, they made change after change. There is one report of Major Pym made in December, 1906. in which he gives about 11 different changes that the Ross Rifle Company had agreed to. There were 8 or 9 more that they thought good but they wanted to know who would pay for them. So we find that many changes were made. The exact circumstances under which the changes were made we do not know. The government contend it was the fault of the Ross Rifle Company and the Ross Rifle Company that it was the fault of the government. But it is clear that when so many changes were necessary the government was too precipitate in entering the contract. It is not necessary to accuse the minister of graft or the contractor of stupidity. It was simply that two men, one of whom had never been a manufacturer of rifles and the other a minister who did not know anything about the manufacture of rifles, attempted at the expense of the country to evolve something they did not understand. The result has been'what we might expect, comnlaint after complaint, and if the case ever got into the courts it would be difficult to say which should be blamed most, the government or the contractor. When they blundered in that way, they changed Mark I and they changed Mark II, change after change was made in Mark I and surely, seeing that, a wise minister would have sat down and decided the kind of rifle he wanted before giving further orders. And yet in March of this year an order was given for 10,000 more rifles. What are the terms of the contract ? The rifles are to be of such a kind as the minister may approve of on or before July 15. That was the contract, an order was given for 10.000 rifles and the minister himself did not know what kind of rifles he was going to have. That again is an illustration that justifies us in denouncing the management of the department in connection with these rifles. Just about this time in the month of May a contract is given to the company | Mr. NORTHRUP.
for 52,000 bayonets at $5.25 apiece. What is the House to think of a contract for bayonets at $5.25 that in England sell for 11s. while the Americans make them themselves for $1.49. Tenders were asked for. How ? Letters were sent to the Ottawa Car Company and the Ross Rifle Company to see if they would tender. Why were these letters not sent to the Chinese laundry companies? Then there might be a dozen peanut stands in the city that would have tendered. Every one knows that they are as likely to tender as the Ottawa Car Company and it seems to be in view of the experience of the government with the Ross Rifle Company, every promise falsified, nothing ever done on time, to make such an outrageous bargain as $5.25 for bayonets, practically without competition is but another illustration of the manner in which this whole contract has been carried out.
I shall yield to the hint of my friend and not occupy the time of the House further. I only wish to say in conclusion that no one can read the evidence taken before the committee and brought down to this House without being impressed with one fact at all events, that if the Minister of Militia or his department, I know not whom to blame, had deliberately tried to prevent any member of this House ascertaining anything about what is going on through a perusal of the files, they could not have adopted a rflore ingenious way of jumbling them up than they did. The first file brought down contained some 1,152 pages. The.first letter in order on that file might be dated 1900 and the next 1905, the next 1906 and the next 1903. A kindergarten could not have more completely jumbled up the files. A letter and the answer of the next, day might be 500 pages apart. It was almost an impossibility to ferret out anything from the file. I call the attention of the House to that fact and wish to have it understood by ministers that when files are brought down in compliance with an order of this House the'1- should be brought down in something like reasonable shape and in chronologic"! order. Those who have had occasion to look into the Ross rifle files have had to spend five times the time that should have been required, owing to the lack of order in the files. Any one could see from the files that there is more in this matter of the .Ross rifle than the minister would imply when lie attacked the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Worthington) as beinr>- disloyal because he is dissatisfied with this rifle. If the minister is right, if the rifle is the best that could be got. and is really a good satisfactory rifle, let us all join hands in making it a popular as well as an effcient rifle. But when I find reports, as I find them, for I have under my hand here 16 or 17 reports from military boards from Vancouver to Halifax, board after board, carefully meeting, taking evidence and sending

in their reports in every case condemnatory of the Ross rifle, I cannot but feel that ail honour must have gone out of Canadian life if all these men have been suborned or ail our influence used improperly, when they all attach the Ross rifle: and when I find the solicitor of the Ross rifle stating before the Public Accounts Committee that whenever he met an English officer he met an enemy of the Ross rifle, I think he made an unfortunate statement for the Ross rifle. It could mean only two things, either that he was rightly an enemy, because he should be, or wrongly an enemy because he had been imnroperly approached and biased. If every English officer is rightly an enemy of the Ross rifle, the sooner we get rid of it and blame the government for introducing it, the better, and if on the other hand, every English officer has been suborned, prejudiced and biased by improper means, so that he is what he should not be. an enemy of the Ross rifle, I for one would lose all confidence in the future of this empire, for I have always understood that an English officer was the synonym for a man of honour. I do not think that is the explanation, I believe that the English officers from their experience for the Ross rifle is well known in England and their knowledge of what has gone on in Canada honestly and conscientiouslv believe that the Ross rifle is not the rifle it is represented to be, not the rifle the people of this country want, and a rifle of which it may be said that the sooner we get rid of it. the better it will be for Canada.
On motion of Mr. Sam Hughes the debate was adiourned.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
We will go on with this to-morrow ?

subtopic: USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS
USE OF TOBACCO BY YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext:
AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce a Bill (No. 173) restraining the use of tobacco by young persons. He said :	This Bill
makes an attempt to meet the call which, to a greater or less extent, seems to prevail iii many quarters for legislation upon the subject indicated in the title of the Bill, the use of tobacco by persons not of mature years. I cannot pretend to hope that the Bill I am presenting will satisfy those who desire legislation which would absolutely prohibit the manufacture and consumption of tobacco in some particular form which is supposed to be more than ordinarily deleterious. To try to meet in some part, at all events, the evil which is complained of,
I am proposing by this legislation to make it an offence punishable by fine, to sell or to furnish to a young person of either sex under the age of 10 years, tobacco in any form for the consumption of that young person himself or herself ; and also to make it an offence on the part of any person to sell, or give, or furnish to a young person under the age of 16 years any cigarettes or cigarette papers for the use of that young person or otherwise. The prohibition accordingly will be upon the furnishing to a young person under 16 of cigarettes for any purpose, and equally upon the furnishing to such young person for his or her own consumption, of tobacco in any form. Then I propose to supplement that prohibition by inflicting a penalty upon the young person himself or herself who commits any offence against the enactments in this measure; a penalty in the first instance, upon conviction, of a reprimand; for the second offence, a penalty not exceeding $1; and for the third or subsequent offence, a penalty not exceeding $4. I thought that some form of money penalty of a comparatively small amount would be, possibly, as far as it would be proper to go in the way of punishing the child himself who committed an infraction of this statute. I have also inserted a clause in the proposed Bill giving any constable or policeman authority under by-law to seize upon and summarily forfeit any tobacco which he finds a young person under the age of 16 years about to smoke, or actually smoking, in any street or public place. There is a clause providing for the case of automatic machines for the sale of cigarettes or tobacco in any form which may be used by nersons under the prohibited age, and a provision exempting persons who may be employed in trade from the prohibitions of the Bill ; also a provision as to the presumption of age, throwing the burden upon the person accused, if he or she appears to be under the age of 10 years, to prove the contrary.
That is the outline of the Bill. I have this further to say, that legislation upon the subject already appears in the statute-books of the greater number of the provinces. I think there is no legislation on the subject in the province of Quebec or in the province of Manitoba ; but in each of the other provinces of the Dominion there is

legislation of some nature with regard to this subject. With regard to age conditions, the provisions of the different provincial Acts differ among themselves. There is no provision in any of the provinces that I am aware of making it an offence on the part of the young person himself to purchase or to consume tobacco, although in some instances there is a provision for the summary seizure of the contraband article. There is, however, since the views expressed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of the Lord's Day legislation in the province of Ontario, room for question whether legislation of this character may not be ultra vires of the provincial legislatures as an encroachment on the domain of criminal law, and in that view, as well as in the view of the fact that the legislation' is in the different provinces of such very diverse character, and that it is applied to different ages, it has been thought better that there should be some legislation of general application to the whole of Canada. For that reason this Bill has been prepared, and I now present it and beg to move its first reading.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called, I feel it my duty to refer to certain statements in reference to myself that appear in the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' of May 20, more particularly as these statements were made after I had given my statement on the subject to the House. In the ' Telegram ' of that date I find several glaring headlines, this one at the top of the page :
Burrows' possessions.
Limits acquired by Burrows, 158G square miles.	_
Then at the bottom of the page :
The Burrows' possessions would span half a continent.
Below this there is a diagram showing a heavy red line on the north side of the Canadian Pacific Railway stretching from Winnipeg to Montreal. Below this there is the following statement:
As stated by H. B. Ames in the House of Commons yesterday, the selected timber limits secured by Theodore Burrows, M.P., brother-in-law of Hon. Clifford Sifton, would if placed end to end, form a continuous strip of thick timber one mile wide stretching from Montreal to Winnipeg.
In other words if Mr. Burrows' limits were flung out in a strip one mile wide it would take an express train two days and two nights to pass from one end to the other.
I want to characterize that statement as absolutely false. It is a slander. Any Mr. AYLESWORTH.
man who gives currency to it, be he a member of parliament or a private citizen is liar and a slanderer. I do not own half the area of timber stated above and which it Is alleged I own, and I have already proven that In this House. I intend to refer to only a few of the statements made in this paper. Here is another false statement:
Since June 6, 1905, Mr. Burrows does not appear to1 have tendered, at least not under any recognizable name.
I say that statement is false and if the man who makes it took the trouble to look at the records he would have known it was false. This newspaper gives my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) credit for having made that statement although I have not noticed it in the report of his speech, but if he did make that statement I have to say that it is absolutely untrue. I have tendered since that time in my own name on timber limits 1282 and 1312. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ames) was very diligent in hunting up the records and having done so he should be fair enough not to make statements like the above aill of which are untrue and have them published all over the country to my detriment and Injury. I feel inclined to apologize to the House for taking up time in referring to these slanderous statements and I would not do so were it not that an occasion of this kind is the only opportunity a public man has to defend himself. Although a great many very unfair and very untrue statements have been made about me during the last six months I have not taken notice of them, and hon. gentlemen will agree with me that I have not intruded on their patience by making personal explanations. Air these false statements are made deliberately to do me injury, personally and politically. However, here is another statement contained in an editorial in this newspaper of the same date, and which says :
His (Mr. Burrows') first method was to send in a tender in the regular form with a space left blank for the amount of money tendered, and two or more certified cheques, one large enough to cover the bids already in, and the other against the contingency of late tenders being received. This was the method usually employed by T. A. Burrows himself.
I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that that statement is absolutely untrue. In any tender which I ever put in, I inclosed the exact amount of my tender and no more. In any tender put in by me it will be found on examination that I specified the amount of my tender. Another statement in this paper is as follows :
On one occasion a berth of 500 square miles was knocked down to the Big River Lumber Company, in which Burrows owned a half interest, for $8,000.

That statement, Mr. Speaker, is also incorrect. The Big River Lumber Company never secured a limit of 500 square miles; they secured a limit of 250 square miles and paid $5,000 therefor.
