speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: AVhen this Bill was up the other evening the question was raised by me as to the provision about the road arrangement. It struck me that, possibly, that ought not to be legislated on here.

I take it that my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) refers to the last clause of the Bill, providing for an agreement between the city of Belleville and the Bridge Company. For many years an agree-

ment between these two has existed by which the city used for city purposes that part of the bridge between their gravel bed and the street, the city keeping that in repair, that is, putting the gravel upon it, for the use of it. That necessitated the making of a new agreement every year. At the city's request the company agreed to put in this clause to make a permanent agreement between them. It does not affect any other interest than that of these two, and both parties assent to it. Therefore, I cannot see that it can do any harm.

I was not objecting to the matter of it, but the question that arose in my mind was whether the province would not take exception to our legislating about an agreement concerning a roadway 5n a city which is a purely municipal matter.

It is the municipality that makes the agreement, and it is purely for the advantage of the city. I am sure the local legislature would not object. Personally, I would not have any objection to the clause being struck out of the Bill, except that I would ljke to protect the interest of the city of Belleville in the matter. All parties interested having consented, it seems to me there is no ground for objection.

I suppose there is really a question about the whole Bill being within the jurisdiction of this parliament. I think the mistake was in bringing the .original Bill here years ago. As all the parties interested seem to be agreeable, I do not wish to raise any objection.

I was absent when the Bill was under discussion before. But I have read the debate which took place on the two occasions, and in answer to the objections made as to this being a purely provincial matter-and not within the jurisdiction of this parliament, I would point out that, even if this Bill were withdrawn, we should still have the same legislation as now exists, which is legislation by this parliament. This does not add to what has been done.
Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Porter) leaving the tolls as tliev are in the printed Bill ?
As they are in the last Bill. These have been agreed upon.
It seems a pity to charge a boy or a bicycle ten cents, the same as an automobile.

The history of the bridge shows that there are very few bicycles passing. This was a compromise. The Bridge Company were asking for an increase of toll on single carriage, horse and driver. But there were so many of these going over the bridge, that it was thought that this would be too large an increase. It was thought that if thev were given an Mr. PORTER.
increase of five cents on a bicycle, the number of which going over the bridge was small, it would appease them to some extent. Everybody is satisfied, and. so far as the bicycles are concerned, it will not materially affect anybody.

House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Fielding for the House to go into Committee of Supply and the amendment of Mr. Worthington thereto.
Mr; FOWLER. Mr Speaker, I will only detain the House for a few minutes to finish the remarks that I was making on the amendment to the motion to go into Supply. The hon. member for Victoria and Halibur-ton (Mr. Hughes) seemed to think that the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Worthington) had done a grievous wrong by making any criticism whatever of the Ross rifle and he said that in no other legislature in the world would criticism of this sort be permitted. The hon. gentleman has forgotten that in the mother of parliaments itself a vote upon the question of the character of cordite supplied to the army of Great Britain led to the defeat of the Rosebery government in 1895. That ought to be a good enough precedent for us to follow in this parliament. Of course I know that the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton has not a great deal of respect for Englishmen and what they do but still I thought that even he would admit that that is a fair precedent for us to follow in the Canadian House of Commons.
. COMMONS
['Supply.']
Would the hon. gentleman mind quoting some authority?

I have just quoted the authority; that ought to he sufficient. The authority is the fact that the Rosebery government was defeated on the vote which I have mentioned

	-

Nonsense.
Mr. FOWLER-in 1895, which is the best possible authority. If a man who is a representative of the people felt that a rifle was being put into the hands of the militia of this country which would be dangerous for the militia to handle it would be a greater crime for him to keep silent than to speak. What are we here for? Are the Minister of Militia and the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton to be the only judges as to the arm with which the militia of this country shall be armed ? If so things have come to a pretty pass. To say that an expenditure mounting into the millions shall be made by this government aud that the members of parliament shall not have the right to discuss the subject of that expenditure is to take a position which is most extraordinary. I think that an argument of that kind needs only to be stated to be refuted; it carries its own refutation with it.
Now, Sir, the question of the cost of this rifle is a matter of some moment to the people of this country. It has been conclusively proved by the gentlemen who have preceded me in discussing this question from the opposition standpoint that the cost of the Ross rifle, even according to the data that we at present have, is about $33.25 per gun; whereas, the average cost of the rifle which it is going to displace, unless an indignant militia refuse to accept the arm, the gun which is supplied by the War Office and which is supplied by private individuals, is only $23.50 per gun. When I speak of the cost of the Ross rifle as being $33.25 I include the cost of the rifle, which is $25, the bayonet, which is $5.25, and the inspection which is $3 per gun, which is the amount according to the expenditure, although tlie Minister of Militia claims that the inspection costs $1.95 per gun. But, for 50.000 rifles they had a vote of $150,000 and almost the whole of that has been expended. Surely they will not deny that these rifles need a very great deal of inspection yet. The cost of the British rifle complete in all its parts, with bayonet and bayonet case, is $23.50, which makes a difference of about $10 on each gun. Some 00,000 of the Ross rifles have been ordered and this makes a matter of $600,000 of loss to this country. For what? For a sentimental idea For some sentimental ideas $G00.000 would not be too much to pay, but -what is this sentimental idea? Let us analyze it. That guns may be manufactured in Canada ? Are they ? It has been conclusively proved,

it lias been admitted, that many of the component parts of this gun are not manufactured in Canada but are manufactured outside of Canada in a foregn country at that. Therefore, we are not paying out this $600,000 for a sentimental idea, but we are paying the $600,000 on account of a foolish contract that was entered into between the Minister of Militia and Defence and the Ross Rifle Company, or Sir Charles Ross, who, I believe, is the Ross rifle company itself. Is it worth it ? That is what the people of Canada will ask. Apart from the question of the danger, which is, after all, the most important question, because you cannot compare a human life with the mere expenditure of money, but, apart from the question of danger to human life from using the gun, because it has been proved to be more dangerous in the hands of the man using it than to the party against whom it is directed, although I believe it did manage to shoot a man the other day in London, is it worth it that we should spend $600,000 for this purpose? That is what the people of the country are asking of this government. The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton has assailed the officials of the general staff. He insinuated that they have been false to their duty, that they have given out some information that was in the possession of the staff to members of the. opposition. I want to say, and I say it on the authority of the hon. member for Sherbrooke that it is absolutely untrue that any member of the staff, that any member of the Militia Department, has given out any information, any secret or private information whatever, to him with reference to this matter. What I say for my hon. friend from Sherbrooke is true also with respect to my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Nortbrup) who spoke on this question last night. It is a very unfair thing for any member of this House to make an attack of that kind on gentlemen who are not here to answer for themselves and on gentlemen who are of the character of those who compose the general staff of the Department of Militia. The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton has told us that the best men in this country are in favour of the Ross rifle, are standing by it and will stand by it. Well, just let us see who are standing by the Ross rifle up to date. There is the Minister of Militia, one; there is the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton, two; the manufacturer himself, three; aud I suppose, when the vote is taken, the majority of the members of this House. The Minister of Militia stands by it-why? He has entered into the contract, he has made this contract, he has to stand by it.
I think I have intimated fairly well the reasons why the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton is standing by it. It is very apparent why Sir Charles Ross, the manufacturer, is standing by it and the majority of the members of this House are

forced by political exigencies to stand by it. The government has entered into the contract.
Those members know in their hearts that it was an unwise contract, that it is an improvident contract, that the rifle is not a good rifle, that the rifle is a worthless rifle ; but they are compelled to stand by the party because the government they are supporting has made the contract and good or bad they must vote in favour of it. Let us see who are the people who condemn this rifle. They are the experts of the Woolwich Arsenal in England ; they are the experts of the musketry school of Hythe, England. These people ought to know something about whether a rifle is good, bad or indifferent, and they have in unmeasured terms condemned this Ross rifle. It has also been condemned by the experts of the Springfield armoury in the United States, who were asked to report on this rifle, and Sir Charles Ross was himself present in 1903 at the Springfield arsenal when the tests were applied to his rifle and when it was found to be wanting and defective. Thus we have the great experts of the United Kingdom aud of the republic of the United States condemning this rifle. Then, in Canada, it has been condemned by General Cotton, the master of ordnance and by Adjutant General Lessard, a member of the general staff, both of whom have reported against it. The officers and men of the militia of Canada have reported against it. The expert shots of the Dominion have reported against it and among others Sergeant Hay-hurst, one of the best rifle men in Canada. The Royal Northwest Mounted Police are opposed to it. On the one hand we have the Ross rifle condemned by the experts of England, and the experts of the United States, and the master of ordnance in Canada, and the adjutant general of the militia of Canada, and the Royal Northwest Mounted Police and the officers and men of the militia. And who have we in favour of the Ross rifle ? We have the Minister of Militia, the member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Sam. Hughes) and the majority vote in this House which for the reason I have given, must sustain the action of the government in connection with the Ross rifle. I do not propose to detain the House any longer. I think the reasons given are amply sufficient why this resolution should be supported. I do not anticipate that those reasons will serve to convince bon. gentlemen opposite that they should vote against the government on this occasion, but when the great verdict of the people of this country is rendered and when the people have a chance to pronounce upon the question, I believe they will condemn the Ross rifle and the government in no uncertain terms.

I desire to say a very few words on this matter.
Every one admits the absolute necessity of supplying the militia of Canada with an effective rifle, because our militia force without a proper arm would be absolutely useless. Therefore, the project to provide a proper supply of efficient rifles for the militia of this country ought to meet with the approval of all. The conditions which faced the Minister of Militia when he had to deal with this subject in 1902 were not free from difficulty. But, the very argument used by the Minister of Militia in support of his course and his explanation of the difficulties that have confronted him during the past six years, afford sufficient reason why he should have paused for a long time before he undertook to engage in the manufacture of a rifle and subject himself to the experience through which he says the English authorities have passed. It is asserted by the Minister of Militia that this was the rifle with which the Austrian army had been equipped since 1896, but the hon. gentleman did not make himself very clear on that point. Is the rifle Mark I which was selected by the Minister of Militia-which I understand to be practically the same as the sample rifle-is that rifle precisely the same as that which has been used by the Austrian army since 1896 ? That phint has not been explained by the Minister of Militia. Now, the hon. minister took a proper course when he called together a board of the best experts of Canada for the purpose of determining whether or not this was a proper rifle, but before doing that it wTas most important that he should have considered whether he could procure within reasonable time for the militia of this country a proper supply of the Lee-Enfield rifles w'hicli are used by the British army. It has been admitted by the Minister of Militia that if it were possible to secure these rifles from the war department in Great Britain or to establish a manufactory in this country for their production, that would be the best course to pursue.
I do not think the minister admitted that.
That is what I understood.
He stated that was his desire, but I do not think he admits such is his intention now.

I did not say so. I said he admitted that if it were possible, there were certain advantages in having the militia of Canada armed with the same rifle as that supplied to the troops of the United Kingdom.
I thought you used the present tense, and said the minister ' admits.'

I did not observe that the minister madie any distinction

between the present and the past tense. The argument has been made by the Minister of Militia that there was great difficulty in perfecting the Lee-Enfield rifle in Great Britain, and the same argument was very properly put forward by my hon. friend from Victoria,, who says that in Great Britain they have Mark I, Mark II, Mark III, and Mark IV for all I know.
Up to Mark X.

The minister therefore had before him the fact that a great deal of experimenting was necessary before any new arm to be adopted for the Canadian militia could be brought to a state of perfection. I should have thought that very circumstance would have caused the Minister of Militia to pause. He was embarking upon the manufacture of a rifle in Canada which his own board on inquiry had declared to be defective in certain respects, and notwithstanding this report the minister approved this rifle in the end without taking any steps, other than the report of Sir Charles Ross himseif, to ascertain whether these defects could be remedied. That was a very unusual course for the Minister of Militia to adopt. He has read the report of that Board of Inquiry. It is not signed by all the members of the Board, but so far as I remember there is not a great deal of difference between the report of the main body of the board and that of the other members. They point out this :
The chief objection or difficulty which was found in connection with the tests to which the Ross rifle was subjected, was brought out in the 'endurance test.' While in firing 1,300 rounds out of each of the rifles, the Lee" Enfield stood the test quite satisfactorily. It was found that after heating, the breech of the Ross rifle closed with more or less difficulty, the action being very stiff with occasional jamming besides which a possibility of double loading ' exists.
Were this an inherent objection to this rifle, independent of details of mechanism, the board would regard it as a very serious matter, but Sir Charles Ross states, that anv difficulty in this respect can be effectually obviated, and the board submit herewith a memorandum (exhibit ' D ') from him in reference to this point which in his opinion, affords an explanation of the unsatisfactory result of this test, and the manner in which the same may be overcome.
The board do not profess to pronounce upon the question of a complete remedy of this objection, but having called attention to it, assume that due precaution and provision with reference thereto will be taken in the event of the rifle being adopted.
The English language could not be plainer for the purpose of placing upon the minister and the government the responsibility of determining that that defect could be remedied and would be remedied before the rifle

was finally adopted. The report continues as follows:
This is all the more important, inasmuch as in comparison with the Lee-Enfield, there is not the leverage in opening the breech which the mechanism of the latter rifle affords.
The magazines of both rifles are unsatisfactory, and can be improved upon. The board recommended the adoption of the ' Harris feed system,' in the adoption of which there need be no difficulty.
Speaking generally, the board believe that the Ross rifle has features which are a positive advantage over the Lee-Enfield, while it is contended by Sir Charles Ross that he can easily remedy any of the drawbacks which have been pointed out.
What reason, after all, was there for the government to abandon the Lee-Enfield ? What were the advantages of abandoning it and adopting the rifle which has been selected ? I do not desire to say one \vord which would reflect in any possible way upon the merits of the Ross rifle, and I do not think my hon. friend the member for Sherbrooke did anything more in his address than to read from the record page after page detailing certain defects which undoubtedly have been disclosed in this rifle. It is asserted that these for the most part have been remedied. Let it not be suggested for one moment that these reports are not important, because the Minister of Militia himself in the concluding part of his speech, speaking of the standing committee on small arms, said this:
I believe these men are able, conscientious and determined to do their duty. Some of them are now at Quebec testing carefully an improved, I suppose it might be called, or a modified Ross rifle. As the result of what has happened; as a result of the reports which have been made, and information which has been gained, the contractor, with the assistance of members of the Militia Department, has thought it desirable to make certain changes, and before the manufacture of the new order for 10,000 rifles is begun this modified form of rifle will be thoroughly tested.
Well, it is of no use for us to say that these reports, which have been read in the House and which formed the principal part of the speech of my hon. friend from Sherbrooke, are not of much importance, in view of the fact that my hon. friend the Minister of Militia has declared that owing to these reports a new, or as he terms it a modified, Ross rifle has been adopted and will be tested by the members of this standing committee before it will be served out to the troops of the country. It does seem to me that the reading of these reports to the House ought not to bring to the hon. member for Sherbrooke the condemnation which the Minister of Militia in the early part of his speech saw fit to mete out to that hon. gentleman.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the rifles now in store are not to be served out until the new rifles are ready ?
No, I did not say that.
Because the rifles now in store are being distributed among the troops and will be used in the present camp.

I made no reference to anything of that kind, because I have no information on the subject. I was merely reading the hon. gentleman's language, and pointing out that in the new or modified form of Ross rifle which is now being tested, those changes have been made as the result of the very reports which have been brought forward in this House by my hon. friend from Sherbrooke. That is the language of the Minister of Militia in dealing with that subject.
In part.
Of course, the hon. gentleman qualifies it by saying that there is other information.

I might point out, if the hon. member will allow me, that the only four important changes that have been necessary in the rifle are a return to four recognized in Mark I as first presented by Sir Charles Ross to the committee.

I do not of course know about that. I do observe in some of the reports that in the first place there was Mark I. Some defects were found in that, and they were remedied, and Mark II rifle was brought out and supplied to the troops. In Mark II certa in defects were found which had not been observed in Mark I ; and Mark III, according to the statement just now made by the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton, is more or less a reversion to Mark I. But what I desire to point out is that the Department of Militia seems to have failed, so far as the evidence before the House shows, to have given much consideration to the defects pointed out by the committee in the first instance.
It would have been worth some further effort on the part of the Department of Militia and of the government to procure the Lee-Enfleld rifle before this series of experiments were entered upon. Great Britain, according to the statements of hon. gentlemen who are authorities on this subject, has been experimenting on the Eee-Enfield rifle for a great many years. Why should not we take advantage of the experience of Great Britain in that regard instead of beginning a similar series of experiments ourselves?-because that is exactly the way in which it has turned out. We have been doing with the Ross
rifle in the last six years exactly the same work which Great Britain has been doing with the Lee-Enfleld in the last ten or twelve years. Was there any need of that? It would not seem so. The Minister of Militia says he was unable to induce the small arms companies of Great Britain to embark in the manufacture of the Lee-Enfleld rifle in Canada.

Might I point out that the Lee-Entield rifle, as it was ii? 1901, when the adoption of the Ross rifle was first considered has changed completely. Practically a new rifle has been adopted in England since then. I think there have been two serious changes in the Lee-Enfleld-not simply changes but new types, two marks, since 1900. We would have had to go on changing just the same even if we had adopted the Lee-Enfleld.

I am not prepared to dispute matters respecting which the minister must be better informed than I.
But it seems to me that the minister's statement supports most thoroughly the argument I have just presented. Instead of beginning a series of experiments on a new rifle ourselves, it would have been more prudent to avail ourselves of the experience of the past in Great Britain as well as benefit by the experience which Great Britain must continue to gather in the future. Undoubtedly the experience of Great Britain must be very much greater than any we could acquire with our comparatively small military force. Great Britain must naturally have a greater number of great men possessing expert knowledge in the manufacture and improvement of arms, who are applying themselves continually to the devising of changes and improvements. I should think that would have been better than to begin the task of doing all that ourselves upon a relatively small scale, without anything like the same number of experts. or men of the same experience in a matter of a highly technical nature, such as this.
Does my hon. friend mean by that that he would have favoured the establishment of a government factory for the manufacture of rifles ?

I would require a little more information than is before the House at present before coming to a decision. My hon. friend, for example, says lie could not procure any manufacturer in Great Britain to start the industry in this country. But he did not inform the House whether or not he offered to any small arms manufacturer in Great Britain the same terms as those he offered to Ross Rifle Com-panv.

The negotiations did not proceed that far. I went to the Chamberlains who, I knew, repre-

sented the Birmingham Small Arms Company, and endeavoured to induce them to come here with a branch factory. They took time to consider and declined.

They might consider and decline the mere offer that they should come to Canada and establish a small arms factory. But they might consider and might not decline a proposal that they should come and establish a small arms factory on the same terms as those tendered to Sir Charles Ross. I am not passing any criticism on Sir Charles Ross in this connection. As a business man, he was perfectly justified in getting the best possible contract he could. But it seems to me that the terms were pretty favourable and such as would be likely to attract the attention of men in England engaged in manufacturing the Lee-Enfield.

I went so far as to state the probable number of arms we would require per year, and I also said I had no doubt the government would undertake to buy all its requirements from the small arms company if they would establish a branch here-those two points being similar to those in the Ross contract.
Mr. R, L. BORDEN. Then of course there is the other consideration whether we could not have secured from Great Britain as large a supply of rifles at any time as we can get from the factory we have established.
We could not at that time get any.

I would be inclined to think, if it were known that the government of Canada required a certain number or nfles per year for a certain period of years, there would not have been great difficulty in arranging with the English government for the supply of those rifles. I would think it would be much easier for the small arms manufacturers in Great Britain to undertake to supply those than for Sir Charles Ross, who had no factory at all, and who had to build a factory.

That is what the Birmingham Company said they would do. but they would have to get the consent of the War Office before making a contract. They wanted to remain in England and supply us here. We wished to have the factory here.
The company, of course, had drawings.

Yes, but they are not referred to in the contract or made part of the contract. Therefore, the contractor is bound only by the agreement to manufacture the rifle up to the standard of the
specimen rifle deposited with the Minister of Militia.
Inspection is provided for.
I understand that. But, if the rifle is inspected and found to come up to the standard, it must be accepted.
Which can be based only on specifications and plans. Inspection would be absolutely impossible without specifications and drawings.

But the difficulty about that is that the minister seems inclined to bring into the contract something that is not there. The proper way, if drawings and specifications are required, would have been either to attach them to the contract or to provide that specifications and drawings should be submitted by the minister, and that the contractor should be obliged to comply with them. That would have left a certain remedy in the hands of the minister which is not available to him to-day.
Then, another unusual provision of the contract, and one greatly in the interest of the contractor, is that the expenditure in manufacture up to $18.75 is to be advanced by the govrenment from time to time. I infer from the evidence that the rifle could not cost the manufacturer more than $18.75. The result of the provision of the contract to which I have just referred, which has been read and which I shall not repeat, is that the government pays for the rifle as it is being manufactured, and that, on its delivery, it pays the profit. This means providing a very considerable proportion of the working capital, a very favourable provision for the contractor.
Another provision is that in case of war, the government may serve a notice of thirty days after which the contractor shall say how many rifles he is able to supply. This seems absolutely illusory. I do not see that the country could depend upon that. Suppose war had been declared between Great Britain and some other country five or six years ago, what would have been our position ? In the first place, our troops would have been armed with Mark I or Mark II of the Ross rifle, and these rifles apparently would not have been perfectly serviceable, for defects are admitted and stated in the reports read before this House. But, passing from that, what would have been our position as to obtaining any necessary further supply of rifles ? How would we stand under this contract as compared with our position under _ some reasonable arrangement with the War Office ? If we had an arrangement with the War Office, we could apply

to Great Britain, who would certainly be the mistress of the seas, and who would be able to bring rifles to our shores. And it is beyond question that an arrangement could have been made for a proper supply within a reasonable time. What would be our position under the contract with Sir Charles Ross. I am not saying this by way of criticism upon him but by way of criticism upon the government for venturing to enter upon such a contract. We should require a further supply of rifles. We would give notice that war had been declared and would call upon him to state how many rifles he could supply. Under the terms of the contract, he could reply : I will supply 1,000 rifles within a year, and if he supplied that number in that time he would fulfil his contract.
He would have thirty days in which to make that reply.
Yes.

But suppose the government said : We want 50,000 rifles, he would have to state how many he could supply. We would at once be able to purchase the balance between the number he was able to supply and the 50,000 wre l'equire.
Ij. BORDEN. That is exactly what I am saying. The minister Is only adding point to my argument. You would be obliged to purchase from some other source.

Certainly.
Mr. R, L. BORDEN. But, so far as Sir Charles Ross is concerned, you would have no guarantee of an adequate supply of rifles in an emergency. That is the point. The contract by its terms failed to make any provision whatever for such an emergency as I have pointed out. If we could purchase 49,000 rifles and Sir Charles Ross could supply only 1,000, what advantage would it be to us? Why not purchase the whole 50,000 from the same source as that from which we would obtain the 49,000 ?
There is a provision under which he is obliged to work double time, if necessary.

I know that. But he is not required by the terms of the contract to supply any particular number of rifles within a specified time.
Now, as I have said, during the course f	"c are obliged to pay up
to $18.oj, that is, <5 per cent of the price of the rifle. We are obliged to supplv that from time to time. We are obliged to supply that upon investigation of the amount expended by Sir Charles Ross, an investigation which does not seem to me to be a very adequate one.

The Minister of Militia corrected me last night, when I referred to this investigation as having been made by an inspector ; it appears to have been made by an accountant. I wras misled by a provision of the contract. In the contract it is provided that the investigation shall be made by the inspector of small arms. But apparently it has been found impracticable to make any such investigation by a mere examination of the material on hand. Therefore an alternative method has been devised, and a chartered accountant employed by the government goes through the books of the Ross Rifle Company, makes a certain investigation and report, and upon that the money is paid over. The contract was unworkable and the substituted arrangement is unsatisfactory. Then there was another important feature of this contract, and that was the grant of about 19 acres of land upon the Plains of Abraham to this company. I do not know what the land was valued at when it was granted, I do not know whether it had any particular market value or not. But I should imagine that it would become of great value in the not distant future. As this practically amounted to a complete alienation of the land, it would have been much more to the credit of the government to follow the usual and constitutional course, and to come to parliament for power to make that grant. The whole project would then have been open to discussion and perhaps to criticism ; whereas under the course which was pursued, a lease for 99 years at a rental of $1 per year, and perpetually renewable, was granted to Sir Charles Ross; so that by means of a perpetual lease the land has effectually passed from the ownership and control of the people of this country without any opportunity for discussion in parliament.
The question of the price of the rifle has been gone into very fully by the' hon. gentlemen who have preceded me, and I will not deal with that again. It appears that the rifles purchased from the War Office in 1895 were purchased for about £2 15s.; the rifles purchased from the trade were of course more expensive. But so far as the price is concerned, we are certainly in no better position to-day, it is not pretended that under the contract we are to be in any better position in the future, than if we had procured these rifles in Great Britain.
Therefore,, so far as this contract is concerned, it has not in any way improved the position of this country' with regard to the armament of our forces. It does not improve the position so far as the character of the rifle is concerned. I would think that is a very moderate statement of the case. It does not improve the position of the country as to the cost of the arm.

The contract itself merely provides that we shall pay at the rate of $25 per rifle, and it is the intention of the contract that we shall pay to Sir Charles Ross exactly the same price as that which we would have been obliged to pay in Great Britain. It does not improve the position of the country in so far as assuring an effective supply of rifles is concerned. The Minister of Militia just now has answered me by saying that if we could not get them from Sir Charles Ross, we could at least purchase them from somewhere else. We could have done that if this factory had not been established. This, taking these three leading aspects of the case, I am not able to see how the position of the country has been improved by this contract.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the action of the government in entering into (this contract, in the first place, without proper investigation of the character of the rifle, deserves the censure of this House. The government took a proper step in the first instance by establishing a board to make a certain investigation, but when that board disclosed certain defects in the rifle, the government absolutely failed in its duty in not continuing that investigation so as to become absolutely assured of its position before it entered into a contract which would bind this country for all time to come. Having regard to the fact that six years have since elapsed, and that during that time'the defects that were then pointed out by that board do not seem to have been remedied either completely or satisfactorily, censure must certainly be laid at the door of the Department of Militia. It may be, as my lion, friend from Victoria and Haliburton has said, that this is to be attributed to some officers in the department. I pass no opinion upon that. But my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton himself, in speaking of the inaction of the department or of its officials, said that as a result every one was condemning this rifle from Dan to Beersheba. Well, if every one was condemning the rifle it was surely high time for my hou. friend the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Worthington) to bring the matter to the attention of the House, and to invite a discussion of the motion which he has presented. I venture to think that the situation to-day is not very desirable or satisfactory. We are paying as much for this rifle as we would have paid for the Lee-Enfield rifle. We will continue to experiment upon it in the future. We have not the same rifle as that which is employed by the British forces, we have not the'benefit of the experience and knowledge gained by the British government in its experiments on the Lee-Enfield rifle, and in time of war we have absolutely no sufficient guarantee that there will be a necessary supply of rifles forthcoming. Under these circumstances, I think the matter has been properly brought to the attention of the House, and that the government, in dealing with the whole subject of the arming of our forces by this rifle, has not displayed the diligence and the knowledge of conditions that might properly have been expected.

I feel like apologizing to the House for speaking at this late hour on a subject which has been apparently so well threshed out. But I am desirous of saying a few words on the subject of this rifle, with which I am personally cognizant, and also of reading a letter or two from some of the people who are interested in rifle shooting in our country. I do not propose to go into the merits of the contract entered into betweeii the Ross Rifle Manufacturing Company and the government, nor am I goiBg into the many questions that have been brought up by the hon. gentleman who moved this motion, and have been spoken to by the Minister of Militia, the member for Victoria and Haliburton and others. I want to relate a little experience I have had myself with the Ross rifle, and also with the Lee-Eufield. I have had considerable experience in shooting, and have been an active member of the Vancouver Rifle Association for some years, and have associated with riflemen on the coast for the last ten or twelve years. I want to say that there are no body of men who are more severe in their criticism of a fire arm than the riflemen; and when they, the formers speakers, speak of every Lee-Enfield as being a perfect shooting weapon, they speak as men who have not had as much experience in rifle shooting and in handling rifles. The good shots, who have won their position- on the provincial teams then on the Dominion team, and from that to the Bis-ley team, trying and retrying rifles that are stored in the different armouries throughout the country. A good shot will come in and look over the rifles that are stacked, and he will select from the armoury a rifle to take out to the range. I have seen Lee-Enfields taken out of the armoury and tried on the range, guns that nobody would attempt to make any correct shooting with. After trying them I think every man who has used the rifle will bear out that statement. Many Lee-Enfields have been given out in times piast and will be given out, as many Ross rifles will be given out. Many Mannlicher. many Ivrag-.Torgenson and many other rifles, no matter what the manufacture may be, which are not perfect weapons in every respect. So that, to condemn the whole Ross rifle outright on account of the bad shooting of one, or two, or three, or even ' one hundred or two hundred rifles, will not

be justified if a fair comparison be msade between that rifle and other rifles. I am of the opinion that the government acted very wisely indeed in establishing a rifle factory in Canada. If it were to carry out the well established principle, laid down many years ago in Canada, that we shall endeavour to manufacture as many kinds of goods as we caD for use in Canada, if it were to follow out the protection policy of our friends opposite, then there can be no argument by or on behalf of our hon. friends opposite against the establishing in Caniada of a rifle manufactory. We, to-day, protect very highly indeed all kinds of manufactured goods. We are endeavouring to bring in manufactures; so that, we are simply carrying out a well established principle of this sand other governments in attempting to bring into the country ail the manufactures we possibly can. Whether or not it was wise to have given the Ross Rifle Company a site on the Plains of Abraham is a question that I am not going to discuss, but I am of the opinion that the people down in the city of Quebec, who are directly benefiting by the establishment of that factory, were willing to see it established ou the Plains of Abraham. So, I do not think that a very good case has been made out on that question. We want manufactures of all kinds in Canada and we want rifles to be manufactured in Canada. If we are ever to be a great nation, as we all hope we will be, we have to undertake all the responsibilities of nationhood and citizenship: so that, when we have established in the country the manufacture of rifles we have made one great step towards our own independence of any other country in supplying us with arms in case we should require them. I must, if I am not too bold, commend the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) for the very fair way in which he has handled this question. He asks: Why did you give up the Lee-Enfield? Why did you go into the manufacture of rifles? There is no more reason in the world why we should have clung to the old Lee-Enfield las there is why Great Britain should have clung to the original Lee-Enfield. I have shot with the old Lee-Enfield and I have seen guns of that make prefectly useless in so far as good shooting is concerned. It may have been a good weapon of offence and defence in the field, but so far as good marksmanship is concerned it was impossible. A great deal of the criticism that bias been levelled against the Ross rifle has emanated from the marksmen of Canada. I tried the Ross rifle three years ago. I went to the butts along with some others and we tried the rifle out there. There was nothing wrong with the mechanism, there was nothing wrong with the magja-zine and there was nothing wrong with the shooting qualities other than this, and it is a point that I immediately brought to Mr. MACPHERSON.
the attention of the Minister of Militia, that the percentage of clear cut marks in the target wsas less than the percentage of those that keyholed. Members of the House who are not used to rifle shooting will not know posssibly what that difference means, but if the rifle ball is the least bit, I might say, wobby, it will make a keyholed shape mark in the target, as the Lee-Enfield never does. It miade a keyhole mark in the target and our shots did not take very kindly to the rifle on that account. However this, like everything else that is being tried, is a new departure and a government or an individual is bound to meet with criticism. If the government or the Department of Militia and Defence, on finding these defects, did not eliminate them they would be justly be targets for the most severe criticism. Mark I rifle, not being a perfect weapon, in so far as the experiments showed, Mark II was issued. The defects in Mark I were overcome by Mark II. Then the defects of Mark II were overcome by (Mark III and that has been the history of any rifle that has ever been given to troops in any part of the civilized world. I want to read a letter that I have received from one of the best shots we have in British Columbia. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the province of British Columbia, per capita, has the best shots in Canada. The rifle team that comes down here to the butts at Rockliffe has done the best shooting during the last five years of any other rifle team in Canada. I speak qf per capita. We. have a man in our province who bias been upon the Bisley team many times and we have also a King's prizeman. Major Duff-Stuart who was one of the original winners of the Palma trophy down at Seagirt is one of the men who favours the Ross rifle. This letter is from Lieutenant James Selater, a gentleman who won the Grand Aggregate last year at the butts in the province of British Columbia and was also well up. not in the first twenty, but in the Bisley team for this (coming year, although he' is not on the Bisley team. Mr. Selater is a well known gentleman in the city of Vancouver, having lived there for twenty years, he was for many years agent of the Canadian Pacific Railway and is now agent of the Western Fuel Company, the Macdonald Marpole Company, as it is called, and is a man of high standing in British Columbia. He writes me this letter unsolicited :
Vancouver, British Columbia, April 25, 1908.
My Dear Sir,-I wondered when I wired you yesterday asking for the new model Ross if you would understand. The message was suggested by Fred. Richardson, who is at present in the hospital here, who had been in communication with Sir Charles Ross concerning a trial of the new gun which I made here. This new model of the Ross is a crack-erjack. You mark my words if in a short

time, when a few of them have been, handed out and the men know what they are capable of, you do not see a demand for them from the militia from end to end of the country. There will be no more knocks, except from some prejudiced ones. I went out last Wednesday along with Duff Stuart and Mr. Studd, of the V.R.A., did not know how the rifle would shoot, or anything about it except that, from our previous experience of which you know, I had no faith in the gun. I was practically a man prejudiced against the Ross. I came away from the range an enthusiast in its favour. It was agreed that I would take two sighters at each range, and then shoot match conditions, with time limit on shots and all other ordinary restrictions. I made the following scores:
200	 33
500	 34
600	 31
Total	 98
and made a ' magpie * with my second last shot at that. With just a little more care I could have had my ' century/ for after I had finished my score I put on three more bulls-eyes just by way of practice. Show me any rifle that a man can do that with for the first time that is not a true weapon. Its straight shooting powers were a revelation both to Duff Stuart and myself. After I had finished the official scores, Duff lay down and put on 34 at 500 and 32 at 600 just as easy as rolling off a log. You ought to have seen the pleased look of wonderment and delight on his face as he plugged in bull after bull, as much as to say * Well, isn't this easy/ He was another convert and Dufl knows a thing or two about a rifle. Since then I have had the rifle out on the range twice and while I did not make 98 with it on account of the weather conditions which were totally against big scoring, yet I made top score shooting against the whole regiment on both occasions, and with no aids to sighting other than the plain sights used on the Lee-Enfield. With the Sutherland adjustable sights the new model ought to he unbeatable. If I continue to get the same satisfaction out of the Ross as I got out of the one owned by Richardson, I shall take it to Bisley and take my chances with them all. Of course I am not an expert on arms and can only speak of what I find. I am more than delighted to know that I am getting one of the new rifles. -Yours,
(Sgd.) J. SCLATER.
That in my opinion, Is as good an argument in favour of the Ross rifle, and a good deal better than any that could be used against it by Sergeant Hayhurst wbo evidently sat down to write out a thorough criticism. I am not casting any aspersion upon Sergeant Hayhurst but I believe that if Sergeant Hayhurst takes one of these new rifles and lies down at the butts, with his sharp eye and steady band he will make such scoriug as be never made before. I believe from what Mr. Sclater says there is no better weapon made. Let me point out this further: the ' News-Advertiser ' of Vancouver is the Conservative organ in 289
that city and it is one of the sanest papers published in British Columbia, and their military writer in his article which appears in the (Sunday issue has this to say of the Ross rifle.
On account of the many criticisms of the Ross rifle, it may be of interest to state that a new model of this rifle has been under test here lately. Staff Sergeant Richardson, the well-known rifle shot, of Victoria, who is at present in the general hospital here, convalescing from a severe illness, purchased one of the new Ross's, hut owing to his sickness was prevented from trying it at the range. It was entrusted to one of the local shots for trial, and a most satisfactory result was obtained on Wednesday of last week. The test was made under the supervision of Major Duff Stuart, the adjutant of last year's Bisley team, who states that the rifle is one of the best shooting weapons that he has ever had in his hands. In the new model a radical change has been made in the barrel, which has been increased both in length and weight resulting in great accuracy in shooting power. The complicated sights of the original Ross have been abandoned, it being the intention, it is understood, of equipping the new model with the Sutherland sight. In the one under trial here, the ordinary ' H ' sight with which the ordinary Lee-Enfield is equipped was attached, so that the results obtained may he fairly compared with those obtainable from a Lee-Enfield. At the 200 yards' range, the score was 33 out of a possible 35. At 500 yards two consecutive scores of 34 were made, and at 600 yards the scores were respectively 31 and 32, all being shot under match conditions. Lieutenant J. Sclater, who assisted in the trial, is so satisfied with the new model that he has ordered one from the Ross factory, which ought to be here in the course of a week. Other improvements than those mentioned above have also been made in the rifle, of which a detailed description will appear later.	,
I might go on for a considerable time showing the merits of the Ross rifle, but I do not think I could add anything stronger than I have read from the letter of Mr. Sclater and from the pen of the military writer in the ' News-Advertiser.' I say this : no matter what department of a government undertakes a new departure they must expect the severest criticism, and, if after five or six years we have succeeded, as we apparently have, in bringing a weapon to such perfection as the new Ross rifle has attained, then I say the money has been well expended and the government is to be commended for the undertaking.

Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIEUX (Postmaster General) There is here an increase of $286,800, which is made up as follows; post office inspector's offices, $12,000; railway mail service, $71,000; post offices generally, $203,000. The increase in the offices of post office inspectors is made up as follows; twenty-six increases of $50 each and one of $30( eleven additional clerkships, and one additional messenger.
What are the duties of inspectors ?

The duties of inspectors are defined in the Post Office Act. Generally the inspector visits all the offices of his district, instructs the postmasters in their duties, looks after the accountant's branch in the several offices, and reports upon their condition to the department at Ottawa. He also locates new offices. He takes the place of the Postmaster General in his district, subject always to the decision of the Postmaster General.
Has he any authority over the time the mails go to different places in the country ?

The inspector is bound to give attention to all these details. When a demand is made for an increased service, the Postmaster General refers the matter to the inspector, who makes a report to the Postmaster General, and then authority is given to him to open an office or otherwise to increase the service.

I wish to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General

and also to the attention of the Minister of Railways a matter which is of great importance to the constituency which I have the honour to represent. Some time ago a railway was constructed from Charlottetown to Murray Harbour. Previous to that time the mail left Charlottetown at six o'clock in the morning and was distributed by stage all along the route to Murray Harbour the day after it reached Charlottetown. I wish to read for the benefit of the minister an editorial which appeared in the Charlottetown 1 Guardian ' of the 15th of May, which will perhaps make the matter clearer than I could express :
Murray Harbour Railway.
There are many complaints of the inadequacy of the train service on the Murray Harbour Railway, and they appear to be well founded. The service is slow and not well arranged. Passengers desiring to leave points along this road and cross by steamer to the mainland under the present arrangements must stay over night in the city both going and coming, and on their return trip must spend not only the night but the best part of the following day here. If a Sunday intervenes the case is still worse.
The mail arrangements by train are equally bad, the incoming mails being held over night and till three o'clock the following day before going out on the train and only reach their destination late the following night at best, and for points a little off the railway not till the third day. This cannot be called modern or up-to-date service. Even under these conditions the traffic on the branch is large and has exceeded expectations. The people served by the road are clearly entitled to a better mail service.
A good while ago it was given out that the Railway Department would put on motor cars for service on this road, but nothing has been heard of this recently. If only one of these cars was put on the Port Vernon loop to connect with the train on the main line it would save an hour in the regular through service. Surely something can be done that will give the patrons of this road a chance to come and go and make connection with the outside world with reasonable promptitude.
Never before were so many millions being expended on transportation, and this we are told is an eleotion year. And yet the train and mail service on the government road through this thickly settled and prosperous" section of the most thickly settled province of Canada is such as we have described. The interests of business, the convenience of the travelling public, the general welfare anu good politics alike demand that this service shall be speedily and permanently improved.
This is a matter which should secure the attention, not only of the Postmaster General, but of the Minister of Railways and Canals. Probably the fault lies with the Minister of Railways. There is np doubt that this is a line of railway which pays the government of Canada perhaps as well as any of. the branch lines connected with the government system, still we have the fact that the mails for the southern portion 289}
of the province arrive in Charlottetown between 9 and 11 at night and are not distributed until three or four days afterwards. It is up to the Postmaster General to improve the system, and I believe, that if this matter had been brought to his attention before, he would have improved it. He should see that we have an up to date post office system in the province, especially the southern portion, which had a better system before we were given improved communication by railway.

I am glad the bon. gentleman has brought this to my attention. The fault does not lie with my department but with the Railway Department, which has the arranging of the railway system of Prince Edward Island. The Post Office Department pays the Intercolonial Railway for mileage just as it does other railway companies, and we are entitled to just as good a service. I shall make the necessary representations to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals to-morrow and see that the Intercolonial Railway gives us a service on Prince Edward Island to which the Island, and particularly that section of Queens county, is entitled.

I am pleased to hear this statement of the hon. gentleman. I do not think however he can claim that the matter has not been brought to his attention. I placed a question on the Order Paper early in the session.
I was away.

I also asked for the correspondence. The question has been brought up year after year, and I trust the minister will take the necessary action now. Heretofore the difficulty was that the Postmaster General laid the blame on the Minister of Railways and Canals, and that minister laid it on somebody else. But if they will both agree, there would be no difficulty in remedying the present condition. That can only be done by giving us a second train ; and if that is done, the hon. minister will be entitled to the gratitude of our people.
Has the hon. minister any inspectors to look after the literature which comes through the mails ?
Every postmaster is bylaw authorized to inspect such literature. He sends the objectionable literature to the department at Ottawa which passes on it in the last resort.
What does the department do with It ?
Burn it.
Is there any inspection of literature which comes from Great Britain ?

Generally speaking, the literature coming from Great Britain is not objectionable. Still last year my attention was brought to some papers which should not be entitled to the privilege of the mail, and through the good offices of His Excellency we prevented it from coming in. I have here a blue-book published by the Postmaster General in England, giving the list of Canadian magazines posted-that is the magazines coming under the special arrangement we made last year with Great Britain and entitled to what is called the intellectual preference. My hon. friend will see that it is very respectable and high class literature.
I have been told that there are many publications coming from Great Britain which should not be allowed in.
Many come in by express.

These are coming in weekly. You can get them in some of the book stores. I went down and picked out half a dozen in one book store. They are the very lowest class of literature, both as regards the printed matter and the illustrations, and should not be allowed into the country. It is the duty of the hon. minister to make some investigation and take some steps to prevent such literature coming in. He knows very well that a great deal of the literature circulated in Great Britain should not be allowed to pass through our mails. You can put your brightest and brainiest in the pulpit and your best young men and women in your Sunday schools, and you may take care of your schools, academies and universities as much as you like, but so long as you have literature of this class filtering into the country, you are going to have the tone of the people dragged down. And when I find the Postmaster General stopping some of the splendid magazines coming here from the United States, the ' Scientific American,' the ' Outlook,' and many papers devoted to industrial education-or, if not stopping them, making them more difficult to obtain by adding to the cost of them in this country-I cannot but note the contrast in this treatment and the treatment of these and the papers of which I complain. So far as the daily newspapers are concerned, the Postmaster was forced to take a different position from that which he assumed at first; and he has paid out tens of thousands of dollars of the public money of this Dominion to daily papers throughout the country because he made the serious blunder in his treatment of daily newspapers in the mails. He made a similar blunder in regard to the weekly newspapers. The weekly newspapers that go from this country to the United States ought not to be saddled with extra postage. It is well

enough for the minister to say that he has placed a man at the border to receive these papers and distribute them throughout the United States, but he will not find the weekly papers satisfied with that. They want a removal of the embargo upon them. Not only are these clean papers, but they do a good work in advertising Canada gratuitously in the United States. The minister knows that he is backing down with regard to these newspapers as he did in the case of the dailies. But instead of coming out squarely and placing them on the same footing as the dailies, he is trying to satisfy them with some little advantage. But the weekly papers are not to be satisfied in that way. They will press their rights until they obtain them.
But my main object in rising was to call the attention of the minister to some of the pamphlets coming into our country.
They do not come through our mails.

But somebody 1ms charge of the literature that circulates in our country. Which of our ministers has control of the investigation of news stands? The newsdealer from whom I purchased these papers of which I have spoken told me that he had fifty publications coming from Great Britain. I picked out half a dozen which should never be allowed to be exposed in this country and the minister knows it well. No matter how they come here, they will have the effect of lowering the tone of our people, and they should not be allowed.
The question to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) has referred is not a new one. I can assure my hon. friend that as regards this periodical, ' Photo Bits '

If the minister will allow me, I refrained from naming any of these publications, because I do not think we should give them any advertising in this House. I would respectfully ask the minister not to use the names.

Very well. As regards this publication which I hold in my hand, it is one of the papers, which, long ago, has been stopped by the department from coming through in the mails. I have myself given instructions with regard to said publications, and every officer in the department with a head on his shoulders, knows that we have a right to stop such literature from passing through the mails. But, when they come in otherwise, for instance, when they come by express direct to the newsdealer, we have not control over them. It is not my duty to watch the news-stands and, when to issue warrants against news dealers. That is the business of the provincial authorities. The duty of the Postmaster General in reference to this class of

literature is clearly defined in the Post Office Act. But, for instance, my hon. friend saw these papers on a news stand. If he had felt it his duty to have a warrant issued against the newsdealer, his course was to go the police court and lay an information. The provincial authorities would, X am sure, sustain his course. The Postmaster General has surveillance over matter that goes through His Majesty's mail, but that is all. In many cases, we have gone beyond the strict letter of our duty in this matter. On many occasions complaints were made to me, for Instance, by the Lord's Day Alliance, and members of the clergy, who lose no time when they find that unwholesome literature is being circulated in the country, in appealing to the Post Office Department. Under such circumstances we give the most positive instructions to the postmasters, and if the papers do not come through the mail, we take upon ourselves to write to the attorney general of the province. On several occasions I have written to Mr. Foy and to Mr. Gouin, and have called attention to the complaints which were coming to the Post Office Department. My hon. friend may rest assured that we have no intention to allow this class of literature to be circulated in the country.
I cannot understand how it is that the Postmaster General can take unto himself the authority of dealing with daily papers or weekly papers coming into the Dominion-
Through the mails.
Well, these do not come through the mails.
They do not pass through the post office.

When they pass through the post office any thing objectionable would easily be covered by a wrapper. There is no reason to suppose that they are coming in by express. Then why is it that he has no power to deal with weekly papers, the filthy papers from the United States ? He admits to-night that the weekly papers can come in here in bulk by express, and be distributed to the news stands, because he has admitted that he has not any control over these publications that are coming in from Great Britain.
My hon. friend surely knows that papers can enter in the form of parcels from England. They come over in a separate compartment of the mail steamer, by express, and they are sold to the newsdealers.
Why not the same over the United States papers ?

My hon. friend knows that, for instance, papers can come from
Buffalo to Toronto by express without passing through the post office. With these, we have nothing to do. Perhaps the Minisister of Customs would have something to do with them. We have a surveillance only over the papers coming through His Majesty's mail. Now, as regards the filthy literature, I take issue with my hon friend when he says that there is a carnival of obscene literature in the Dominion, any one would infer from his words that this kind of literature is being spread all over the Dominion. From the reports we have it appears that the bulk of periodicals come through the mails, and it is only in exceptional cases that they come by express. But as regards papers coming through the mails,
1 can assure my hon. friend, from the reports I have from the officers of the department, and from my own experience in dealing with these matters, that since the amended convention came into force last year in the month of May, we have practically purged the mails. If my hon. friend will not take my word for it, I would ask him to inquire for instance from the very zealous association in the province of Ontario known as the Lord's Day Alliance ; let him ask the members of the clergy. We have received many letters from those associations in Ontario and other provinces thanking the department for the course we have followed on that question. This paper surely does not come through the mails, it started throught the mails, but we stopped it There are four or five obscene papers of the same class and with about the same title coming into Canada. But when those papers are being sold, any citizen can lay a complaint, can have a warrant issued and a fine imposed on the newsdealer who sells them. But that citizen must himself put the judicial machinery into motion.
Some minister must be responsible for this literature that is coining in. Perhaps it is the Minister of Customs, who has been looking at one of these papers for a little while.

My hon. friend may find the evidence in the blue book which I handed to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), that as soon as we make representations to the post office authorities in Great Britain as to the objectionable nature of any of the newspapers which have applied to be put on the Canadian post list, they immediately withdraw the privilege which is given those papers, that is to say, the privilege of coming into this country at the reduced rate.
I would ask the minister if he did not forbid ' Collier s Weekly,' the 'Scientific American' and some other United States publications from being expressed into this country and dis-I tributed here ?

No. The weeklies from the United States were coming in with a mass of other papers, good, bad and indifferent. They were filling our mail cars, they were paralyzing the whole mail service. It was not the desirable papers that were coming in in such large quantities, but mere advertising sheets which under cover of a journal, contained nothing else but advertisements, and sometimes very-filthy advertisements ; novels and novelettes. As I have explained to the House time and again, we objected to that. We said, the time has come when we must control our own classification, that is to say, the papers that should be admitted into our mails coming from the United States must be of the same character as the paers published in our own country and enjoying the second class rate. The Americans were not averse to that; they were themselves deluged by so-called papers loading down their mails and had been for years. Representations were made, and finally it was agreed that these papers should come from either country at a rate not less than four cents a pound. Now my hon. friend says : You have departed from your cast iron rule, you have backed down, you have not been consistent. Let me tell him that the objection was not against the dailies. The daily papers published in the United States and sold in Canada are not objected to.

Why is it if the daily papers are not the objectionable papers that are coming into this country the minister has been compelled to pay tens of thousands of dollars of the people's money for the mistake that he made last May ?
No.
Well what has the minister done ?

My hon. friend must not give himself to the-shall I say virtue- I dare not say vice-of exaggeration. He should not exaggerate. We had first to come to definite terms. We said that papers going out from Canada to the United States, or papers coming from the United States to Canada and enjoying second class mail privileges, would have to pay four cents a pound-dailies and weeklies included. We make no distinction in regard to that certain rule. My hon. friend asks : How is it that you have paid back to the papers thousands of dollars ? Here is what happened :	Very few American daily papers are read in Canada. On the other hand some of our newspapers are sold in large quantities in the United ' States, especially in the eastern states, and also in Michigan and Ohio. The Winnipeg ''Free Press,' the Toronto ' Daily Mail,' the Toronto ' Globe,' ' La Presse.' ' La Patrie,' ' Le Canada ' considered themselves somewhat mulcted when that new regulation was put into force and as our objection was not against the daily newspapers and as they

were bona fide papers falling under our classification, publishing political news and giving the ordinary food which one might expect in a daily newspaper, we relaxed the rule and we stated that our amendment to the convention would not apply to them. When we amended the convention last year the Canadian Press Association met at Toronto, and, whilst we were patriotic enough not to object too strongly to the new convention as amended, yet, it appealed to the Postmaster Generai and asked that it should not exact the difference between the old rate and the new rate until the first of January. That representation was made to me by all the papers, the ' Daily Mail and Empire,' the Toronto ' Globe,' ' La Presse ' of Montreal, the Winnipeg ' Free Press,' having a circulation in the United States. The editors sent a delegation to Ottawa and they said : You should not exact the difference between the old rate and the new rate until the 1st of January next. The change took place in the month of May last. Well, I said to the representatives of the Canadian Press Association :	First of all, be
good enough to pay according to the new rate and on the 1st of January I will ascertain if really you have been taken by surprise and on the 1st of January, if my colleagues agree to it, I will see that a remittance is made. Was not that fair and was not that good policy ? They reported to me that the notice had not been sufficient. According to the postal convention between the United States and Canada a public notice of some months has to be given that an amendment will take place or that the convention will be abrogated. The newspapers said : We did not pay attention to that ; we did not see it. Wo were in ignorance of the amendment and it has taken us by surprise. Under these circumstances I reimbursed them the difference between the old and new rate on the 1st of January next. That is what has been done and there has been no complaint against it.
I may be very dense but I cannot quite understand this. On May last the minister places a restriction on daily and weekly papers going into the United States.
And coming from the United States.

And also on papers coming from the United States into Canada. Now he has receded from that position. He takes back all that he has done in regard to daily papers and in taking back what he has placed on the statute-book he allows every daily paper in the United States to come into this country just the same as they did two years ago. The same daily papers are coming as they came two years ago.
There is no objection to them.

Why did not the minister investigate the subject last May and satisfy himself before he put the daily papers to all the inconvenience that they have been put to for a year, the loss of subscriptions and the loss of thousands of dollars that he has paid back. He must admit that he has paid that money out without getting any value for it. I would suggest to the minister that instead of only backing down part of the way in connection with the daily papers he should come out and say, I have made the same kind of blunder in regard to the weekly papers and I will do the same thing ; I will pay them for the mistake made last May.

I cannot be so angelic as to admit that I have made the blunder that my hon. friend suggests I have made. I confess that I am but human, but still under the circumstances I have done the best and events have proven that the policy was on the whole a wise one. As regards daily newspapers,, there was no complaint, but we had at that particular moment to apply the rule to all newspapers whether weeklies or dailies. I hSave outlined briefly to the House the arrangement I have made with the Washington authorities and I think it is a fair arrangement as regards the weeklies. I may now state fully how the whole question stands :
The interchange of second class matter between Canada and the United States is now effected at the rate and regulations herein stated.
Under the postal convention between Canada and the United States, as amended in January last, and effective since February 5 last, legitimate daily newspapers published in either country, and addressed to bona fide subscribers in the other, may be mailed by the publisher in the post office at the place where they are published upon prepayment of postage in cash at the rate of one cent per pound or fraction thereof.
Newspapers and periodicals published less frequently than daily, when posted in either country for despatch to the other, are liable to postage at the rate of one cent for each four ounces, or fraction thereof, calculated on the weight of the package for each post office of destination, and when thus mailed direct prepaid by stamp the country of destination is under obligation to effect distribution of whatever may have been accepted by the country of origin.
United States legitimate newspapers and periodicals, other than dailies, which have been accepted by the Post Office Department of Canada, may, under the mailing-m-Camada privilege upon prepayment of postage ait the rate of one cent per pound, be posted by United States publishers at the following Canadian post offices, viz.: St. John, New Brunswick; Montreal, Quebec; Toronto, Ontario; Winnipeg, Manitoba; Calgary, Alberta, and Vancouver, British Columbia. Copies to be so tendered for mailing must be despatched
to Canada by express and be restricted to bona fide subscribers. Publications admitted under the mailing-in-Oanada privilege must comply with the provisions of the Postal Law of Canada, that is, in their subject matter they must f consist wholly or in great part of political or other news or of articles relating thereto, or to other current topics.'
Canadian newspapers and periodicals issued less frequently than daily may be posted in the United States upon prepayment of postage at the one cent per pound rate. United States regulations governing the mailing in that country of a newspaper or periodical published in another country expressly stipulates that copies of a publication so mailed, in order to be accepted at the one cent per pound, rate of postage, must he posted by the publisher's authorized agent, and in accordance with this regulation it would be necessary that the Canadian publisher have an authorized agent in the place at which he desired that his publication should receive entry into the United States mails as second class matter. Recently, however, this regulation was modified to the extent that eleven United States post offices have been exempted trom requiring that the posting should be performed through a publisher's agent. relax that regulation and the postmasters will be the authorized agents for these *weeklies.
