If these objectionable newspapers which are to be seen here do not corue through the mails then I presume they must enter through some customs port. I realize that there might be a great deal of difficulty for the Minister of Customs to exercise any very effective control or supervision over the entry of such papers.
We have the power.
I do not wish to prolong the debate, but I see the minister is letting himself down as easily as possible.

I should have pointed out that we have secured what I may term our independence in connection with postal matters. I will admit, to please my hon. friend, that I have receded on the dailies and that I have receded to some extent on the weeklies.
Hear, hear.

But we have gained this very important point that we will only admit to His Majesty's mails in Canada the newspapers that will come within the Canadian classification. Prior to the recent amendment to the convention -we were obliged, under the reciprocity as regards posted matters, to accept a huge mass of filthy weeklies, objectionable literature, and patent medicine advertising sheets. Now, we accept only such as come under our own classification and that is a great advantage to Canada.
How are you situated m regard to publications from Great Britain ?

Newspapers published m Great Britain can come to Canada at the reduced rate of 2 cents instead of 8 cents per pound. We can stop objectionable literature from Great Britain as well as from any other country. ,
Previous to the convention did we not have the same right with respect to similar periodicals coming from the United States ?

I understand that the Minister of Customs has the power. I do not want to minimize the importance of exercising the power effectively. Whether these papers come in by mail or by express they are equally objectionable and ought not to be exhibited for sale on the public news stands of the country. I would like to ask the Minister of Customs whether the matter has come under his consideration in any way, what means he has exercised in the past, and what further means he can exercise in the future, to prevent the entry of periodicals of this character, which I am sure he would consider very objectionable indeed.

I do not censor these publications myself ; my officers do that-One of the publications I saw is something that I think should not be allowed to come in. We are continually confiscating literature of this kind. Every little while in Montreal we are not only having literature seized but having the importers of it brought up and fined. I was not aware that such publications were coming from Great Britain, but I will mention the matter to the officer in charge. Under the law we have perfect power to order literature of this kind to be destroyed. Whether we would have power to confiscate anything of this kind after it had passed the customs and gone into the possession of the dealer I do not know. That is a point on which I shall have to consult the commissioner. Perhaps the leader of the opposition will have an idea whether under a tariff that prohibits immoral literature we could follow it after it had passed the customs. I am inclined to think we could.

The object of the amend ment was specially to restrict the objec tionable literature coming from the Unite states which Game here in vast quantities and particularly to restrict these advertis mg sheets which came under the guise o newspapers and which were to be found ii almost every home in the country.
The minister wouh seem to think that these sheets do no come through the mails now.
I know that some of them have been prevented from the verv beginning. * .	,	,	-y

It would depend altogether on the terms of the statute, and I am not sufficiently familiar with these to give any opinion on the subject. It would seem to be a fairly logical consequence that if the goods are prohibited, and through some inadvertence of an officer and the impossibility of detecting their true character, the goods are permitted to enter the country, the customs or some other department should have the power to follow them up and see that they are taken possession of and destroyed.

I know that the Minister of Customs and the Postmaster General will do what they can to stop the im-

portation of this kind of literature, which is exposed openly on the news stands. 1 picked up this paper yesterday at a news stand, the proprietor of which told me that he received fifty publications every week from the old country. These publications are coming in in very large quantities and are being distributed throughout the country. I think some of them come by mail, because an ordinary small newsdealer could not afford to get them by express from the old country. The newsdealer told me that Saturday was the day on which these publications were first exposed for sale, so that when I bought this paper yesterday, the bulk of them have been sold. I may say that I have spent a great deal of time in the United States, travelling and going to school in different cities, and X can defy the Postmaster General to go into any city of the United States and pick up any such literature as this. I do not believe it is allowed to be published. X cannot express too strongly the hope that the ministers who have charge of this matter will stop the importation of this kind of stuff, and they cannot stop it too soon.

My hon. friend has spoken of the facilities provided for newsdealers to import this objectionable literature through the mails. It is quite true, it may come in small packages, and be easily passed without being detected ; but the Postmaster General has the right to open the packages and see whether the literature is objectionable or not. If it is, he confiscates it. I remember a case in point in Montreal. A certain newsdealer in St. Catherine street was selling a very objectionable newspaper which he received through the mails from Paris, France. My attention was called, by the Archbishop of Montreal, to these importations. I immediately informed the postmaster at Montreal to stop them. He did so, and to his great surprise two weeks afterwards he saw in the same news stand the very papers which he had stopped coming bv mail. Then he found that the newsdealer had changed his mode of procedure and was receiving the papers by express. When objectionable newspapers are offered for sale, any citizen can take action under the Criminal Code and have a wararnt issued, and the law is pretty severe against the circulation of immoral literature. If my hon. friend will allow me to read the regulations of the Post Office Department on this subject, it may serve some good purpose:	.
According to regulation 191 it is forbidden to post for delivery or transmission through the post any obscene or immoral book, picture. lithograph or other publications, of an indecent, seditious or scurrulous character, or any letter or envelope, or post card or wrapper upon which there are words or things of the character aforesaid or tending
to injuriously affect the commercial or social standing of the persons addressed. There is not a day when I do not receive a dozen or so objectionable post cards sent me by clergymen and other gentlemen throughout the country complaining of the circulation through the mails. In each case the decision is prompt, but of course we cannot foresee that people will send indecent post cards through the mail. The regulation 195 provides for the treatment of correspondence by persons engaged in illegal business.

The prohibitive articles in the tariff cover books, printed papers, photographs or representations of any kind of a treasonable, seditious or indecent character. The difficulty consists sometimes in determining that a certain case comes within that category.

The difficulty lies in the application of the clause. Of course when a publication is clearly immoral there is no difficulty. But there are papers that circulate socialistic ideas and I am hammered from all sides to prevent their circulation. We have of course to be very careful about infringing on the liberty of the subject; that is our great tribulation.
I notice an expenditure in the Yukon of $100,000, and the income only amounts to something over $11,000.

We have to give proper facilities to all sections of the country, and in the Yukon territory our service is much more expensive than in any other section. Even with the sum we pay in mail subsidies and otherwise to the railway and steamship companies, we are obliged during the winter months to forward only a certain weight of mail. I was interviewed the other day by the representative of the White Pass Railway Company, and he told me that in the future they could not renew their mail contract with the department, although we pay them a very high price. Whereas in previous years they would give us three or four trips a week, in the future they will only give two. The reason they give is that business has decreased during the last few years, the cost of living is very high, the roads are much more difficult, and the space available and the numbers of cars and steamers are less.
Does that include transportation to Dawson city ?
Yes.
How much is spent by the postal department in the Yukon outside of transportation ?

The Dawson post office, $4,425. The postmaster's salary is $3,750

and $657 allowance for rent. That is not very much.
X do not want to go into the details.

Well, the biggest figure is for travelling expenses of inspectors and clerks, $12,440. Then we have the post office at White Horse, $3,150. That is where all the mail matter aggregates during the winter to leave again when navigation opens in the spring.

transportation, the best man available. Sometimes people claim to have a title to a position because they have been in the service for a long time. The gentlemau who acted as railway mail superintendent in New Brunswick died some time ago.
Two years ago.

No.

I know the case
I am not asking about the case, but about this expenditure.

I will explain. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) -knows that when a postal clerk is charged with robbery of the mails, to establish our case we must prove that the letter has been posted at such a place and received at such a place.

The clerk was somewhere around Moosejaw or Calgary I think. The trial took place in the fall of the year and was postponed once or twice. We couldn't ; they had to be brought there.

Montgomery. Ottawa ; Tackaberry and Laurie, London : T. Thompson, Toronto ; Mrs. T. O'Donohoe, Montreal ; H. L. Carson, Ottawa ; E. Brown, St. John, New Brunswick. They belong to a different category, they are very small bags.

Some time ago I drew the attention of the Postmaster General to the condition of the post office at Macleod.
I would like to know if he has any report from that office, or if anything is being done to provide better accommodation. I make no complaint with regard to the management of the office, only with regard to the lack of accommodation.

My hon. friend drew my attention some time ago to the state of the post office at Macleod, and I immediately wrote an official letter to our inspector in that district, and I also wrote to the Minister of Public Works calling his attention to the matter. In many of the cities and towns of the province of Alberta, post offices which were quite sufficient three or four years ago, and even two years ago, are to-day altogether inadequate to the increased population. When representations are made to me of the need of better accommodation, I pass the matter over to the Minister of Public Works. The Post Office Department decides if the building is necessary and the Public Works Department erects the building.
The accommodation is entirely inadequate, and I hope there will be no delay.
Have any post offices been closed during the last year in the province of New Brunswick, and particularly in the county of Kings and Albert ?

I do not know that any have been closed in that district. Post offices are closed only in case there are no more patrons, or because a postmaster cannot be found, or because there is no sufficient reason for maintaining the office. Does my hon. friend say that any office has been closed?
There is the Kerry office in the county of Albert.
If there are twenty or twentydive people I would open an office at once.

Then I call attention now to the post office at Kerry, and beg the minister not to close it. If it is closed, these people would have to go a very long distance for their mail, some of them perhaps ten miles.
Does the minister buy the clothing for the uniforms and have it made up afterwards by other parties?

We buy the clothing ourselves, and the contractors here at Ottawa. Noel and iChevrier, make the uniforms under our supervision. We have an officer in the department who supervises the making of uniforms.

I see you purchased from Caldwell, Boyd and Company, Lanark, a quantity of material; and the Crown Tailoring Company of Toronto make up a large number of trousers, uniforms and so forth.

Do you buy the material from Caldwell, Bovd and Company, and send it to Toronto to be made up?
Yes.
Then the Bill of the Crown Tailoring Company is simply for making the goods, not furnishing material. For instance, that $3 for making up trousers, is that for the stuff and the making?
I think that is the price of the making, not of the stuff. The blue melton trousers, I think that is for the cloth and the making.
I presume it would be the same with the tunics. They charge $5.45, that is a pretty round price for making the tunic if they do not find the stuff. Do you put this up to public tender?
Yes.
On page J-2 of his own report, the hon. Postmaster General has paid $52,000 to the American Note Company for stamps. Does he ask for tenders for these stamps ?
Yes, there is a contract with the government passed by my hon. frieDd the Minister of Finance.
How long does it run ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Tenders were asked for originally and this contract was extended.
For how long ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it was for a period of five years more.
Were new tenders asked for ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not recently. This is a class of work for which you have difficulty in getting tenders. There are but few persons able to compete, and by gelling tenders you accomplish nothing. The course adopted was that originally tenders were invited and the contract 'went to the lowest tenderer. This contract was extended on two occasions. In both instances the proposals were referred to the King's Printer and in one instance to a gentleman associated with or interested in the printing of bank notes, familiar with the value of these goods and upon the certificate of the King's Printer that the prices were fair and reasonable, the contract was extended.
I would like to ask the minister if he has ever taken into consideration the question of printing postage stamps and bank notes at the mint. I think that is worthy of his consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The facilities there are not at all adapted to it. My hon. friend Mr. FOSTER.
means that we should have a government printing establishment instead of the present arrangement. The present arrangement of not having this work done in a government establishment but in an office in the capital specially constructed for the purpose and more or less under the supervision of the government was adopted some years ago and it has worked satisfactorily.
The original contract was passed in March, 1897. They print Dominion notes, postage stamps, postal notes, post cards and inland revenue stamps of every description.

There is an item of $21,000 and over at page S-61 for ' labour at the Montreal post office.' What is the class of labour that you employ there ? It seems a large amount of money. I suppose there is a good deal of work to do.
Mr. LEMIEL'X. The two largest offices in the country are Toronto and Montreal. We have in Montreal, more than anywhere else, the burden of the foreign mails. The mails are distributed from there to all points in the country. Therefore, we have to employ more transfers and more labourers than at any other office, Many of these labourers are not civil servants in the ordinary sense of the word. They are merely labourers and their wages range from $1.25 to $2.25 per day. Besides that we have in Montreal and Toronto a very brisk Christmas season when we are obliged to employ 100 men or more in order to provide the public with the necessary facilities.
I notice that in Toronto the pay of labourers ranges from $1.25 to $1.75 and in Montreal from $1 to $2.25.
The farther west -we go the dearer labour is.
But in Montreal it is dearer than in Toronto.
Labour in Calgary and other western towns is higher than in Montreal, Halifax and St. John.
In Vancouver it is from $1.25 to $2.

There is no section of the country where we have to change our labourer and mail clerks more frequently than in the west. That is our great trouble. They complain that the salary is not high enough. We give them a provisional allowance besides.
But for these labourers you do not have any provisional allowance. You do not mean to say that you are paying less in Vancouver than in Montreal ?
That is a guess that the minister has made.
Generally speaking, we pay more.
That does not seem to be a satisfactory explanation.
Why do you not say that it is a better class of labour in Montreal ?
I wish I could say that.

I have received a great many complaints from Montreal. I do not suppose there is another city in which the mail service seems to be as badly managed as in Montreal. The minister is well aware that not only are the daily papers complaining constantly, but business men are complaining and thirty members of the board of trade have signed a statement setting forth their complaint. I cannot understand how it is that from a city like Montreal there should be so many complaints constantly of irregularities, of miss-sent letters and of all kinds and classes of complaints.

I will admit that up to a year or so ago there were many complaints from Montreal. I have explained before to the House the reason why. There were some internal difficulties in the Montreal post office, difficulties which have been removed since the appointment of a very efficient officer, Mr. Gaboury, who is the assistant postmaster. There are not so many complaints as my hon. friend thinks. If there is a missent letter I know it because there is a wire or a letter sent stating the fact. It is surprising how few complaints are made. I will give the committee a statement about the complaints that are made. The total number of complaints relating to the carriage of articles through the mails last year was 708. There were 573 complaints of delay and with respect to 251 of these the evidence showed that the delay was due to causes beyond the control of the department. Last year the winter was very severe especially in the west. We had a coal famine and while trains were not running complaints should have been made to the weather bureau and not to the post office. When trains v ere stopped letters were delayed and the complaints came to the Post Office Department. They should have gone to the weather bureau. There were 48 complaints of misdelivery and in 8 of these the responsibility rested elsewhere than with the department or the misdelivery was not established. There were 84 complaints of nondelivery and in 47 of these the complaints were not substantiated by evidence, or the sender and addressee and not the department was at fault. It should be born in mind that 478,290,967 articles of mail matter were carried by the Post Office Department during the same period. The complaints numbered only an infinitesmal fraction of a percentage of the total number of mail pieces carried so that the statistics would not confirm the statement that the post office is not well managed. Men are not perfect, letter carriers are not perfect, the department may sometimes be at fault, but it is surprising that compared 'with the vast business the complaints were so few.
The hon. gentleman does not hear one half of the complaints.
If they are from my hon. friends district he does not fail to mention them.

I have made complaints many times but there are a great many others I have not made. For instance there was a letter posted to a member of my household from Winnipeg and it went to England and back again.
Was an investigation made ?

No. The letter was properly addressed and the mistake evidently occurred in the Winnipeg post office. The practice in England is to bring all these complaints before the Postmaster Genera!, but in Canada there is a feeling that people do not like to complain as they imagine they might get some official into trouble. However that may be, the Postmaster General does not hear a very large proportion of the complaints.
Will there be a probability of my getting the Customs estimates through when this item is passed ?
I do not think so.
I am tired sitting here and I will go home if you do not think my estimates will be passed to-night.
I thought you were interested in the Postmaster General's estimates.
If you do not take the Customs estimates up to-night we are out of money and it is a very serious thing.
I have often felt that way myself.

I notice that the report of the Post Office Department states that in the dead letter branch the value of contents of letters received during the nine months ending March 31, 1907, is estimated at $524,000 while the amount disposed of was estimated in value at $34,000. What is the explanation of that ? Does it mean that the Postmaster General has letters to the value of nearly $524,000 still in his possession.
Yes, less the $34,541 disposed of.
What do you do with them ?
They are in our possession and we have not been able to dispose of them.
Are they registered letters ?
No, it includes parcels and all sorts of things.
You auction these off, do you not ?
Yes.
How often are these sales held ?
I could not say.
Has the minister ever taken into consideration the question of issuing a special stamp, part of the postage of which could be used to assist in the fight against tuberculosis ?

My attention was called to an article which has been published in the ' Outlook ' by a celebrated philanthropist of the United States in regard to a stamp which has been Issued every year at Christmas time in Denmark, if I mistake not, and sold for two or thi-ee weeks during the year. It has a special value of say five cents, while the value of the ordinary stamp is two or three cents, and the difference goes to the hospital for the suppression of tuberculosis.
Are people obliged to buy that stamp during that period ?
No, it is purely voluntary : but in Denmark it has been a tremendous success. Everybody is anxious to have a stamp.
Is it purchased as a souvenir ?
Oh, yes. People wish to have it on their letters and parcels that are sent abroad.
But if a two-cent stamp is used on a letter, it will go just the same ?
Yes. The use of this special stamp is not compulsory. Of course, I have not studied the question for Canada, but it has been hinted to me that such a stamp might be issued.
I understood that last year the minister was giving this matter consideration, and had some idea of issuing the stamp for last Christmas. I would like to know if he is seriously considering it now.

Oh. yes. the matter is under consideration, and very serious cou-Mr. ARMSTRONG.
sideration. The reason that this year I ceased considering it was that I decided to issue a series of stamps to commemorate the Quebec tercentenary, and it would not do to multiply these special stamps. In fact, the postal union would, I am sure, protest if a country abused the privilege. But I may assure my hon. friend that after the tercentenary stamp is issued, I shall be pleased to take the earliest oportunity to confer with him and all others interested in regard to that matter, always subject to the approval of my colleagues.
Why should the postal union object ?

The simpler and more uniform the stamp is, the better for the postal relations. Up to the last postal union congress, memorial stamps, such as those that will be issued for the tercentenary next month, could be used from Canada to any other country. By the regulations adopted at the last congress, it has been stipulated that these special stamps shall be used only on the continent; so that the stamp to be issued for the Quebec tercentenary will be used only on the continent of America, unless I obtain permission from the British authorities to use it between Canada pnd Great Britain, a permission which I expect to obtain. According to the postal union rules the special stamp cannot be used between one continent and another.
I would like to ask if the revenues from this special stamp go into the ordinary revenue of the Post Office Department, as we are voting so much money for this celebration.

Of course, parliament has voted $300,000 towards the Quebec tercentenary. The stamps, I hope, will be sold in large quantities ; but we must also provide for the extension of the postal service year by year in Canada. Of course, the extent to which these stamps will be sold is entirely speculative. But I can say that the stamp to be issued next month under the authority of the present Postmaster General will be from an artistic point of view one of the most beautiful ever issued.
Can the minister give us an idea of what the design will be ?

I cannot, because it is contrary to etiquette in such cases to publish the description beforehand. But I intend, as soon as the time is ripe, to lay on the table of the House a whole series of the stamps, so that the members can see for themselves the kind of stamps we issue in celebration of that great occasion.

How is it the Canadian Pacific Railway receive about $550,000 for the nine months, the Grand Trunk Railway $289,000 and the Intercolonial Railways $120,000? I notice that the Intercolonial

Railway is paid bulk sums in many instances for carrying the mails and the Grand Trunk Railway also for a number of places, while the Canadian Pacific Railway furnishes a definite statement and charges so much per mile, varying from two cents to eight cents. On the Intercolonial Railway there is paid between certain places from four cents to eight cents.

In the United States they pay according to space and weight. Here we pay according to mileage. The standard price is four cents per mile for baggage car service and eight cents a mile for postal car service, the postal cars being equipped with racks for boxes and letters and accommodation for mail clerks. The Grand Trunk Railway was the first railway system built in Canada and it received from the government a special rate on certain lines per mile or per weight. That system went on until Sir Oliver Mowat became Postmaster General in the fifties before confederation. Sir Oliver Mowat appointed a commissioner, and that commissioner fixed the mileage system which is still in existence. The Grand Trunk Railway had some vested rights because it was the first company carrying mail, and it has kept those rights until now, but at the period I have mentioned, a four cent per mile for baggage car service and eight cents per mile for postal ear service was made uniform on the other railways. Later on, it was made uniform on the new portions of the Grand Trunk Railway. The Canadian Northern, which was built still later on, when It was voted subsidies, -was given these subsidies on condition that it should carry the mails free. In the Subsidy Act, there is a clause providing that railway companies receiving subsidies from the government shall carry the mails free. I cannot say in what year that clause was inserted. At all events we have had lately a protest from the different railway companies that the amount paid is not high enough, and I will ask council to appoint a commission to look into the whole question. The principle has been practically adopted that a revision must take place every ten years.

I cannot understand why from one little town to another two cents per mile should be charged and in other cases four cents per mile. Take page S-19 of the Auditor General's Report and you will find that from New Germany to Caledonia twro cents per mile is paid the Halifax and Southwestern. On the next page you will find that eight cents is paid from Lunenburg to Middleton. Then the Dominion Atlantic is paid from Truro to Windsor one cent per mile and from Halifax to Annapolis eight cents per mile. There must be some explanation of these differences.

Generally speaking the rates are eight cents and four cents. Sometimes, however, requests are made for more frequent service, and the arrangements is an arbitrary one as the department finds that the revenue does not always warrant the payment of an additional subsidy.

Look at the Intercolonial Railway, page S-20, it is paid $121.000. In some eases bulk sums are paid and in others so much per mile. I can understand that during the summer months more money be paid to the Intercolonial Railway, but it seems strange that that road should get $121,000 when the Grand Trunk Railway only receives $289,000 on all its systems.

The Grand Trunk came at a time when a special arrangement was made. They were the only railway, and contracts were based on a lower figure because money was worth more in those days than it is to-day. That is why they ask for a revision of the subsidy.
Do you ever get registered letters in the dead letter office ? If so, what do you do with them, when you cannot locate the addressee?
We retrace, if possible, the person .who sent the letter. If we are unable to find either party, the money goes to the Receiver General.
In this amount of $524,000, in the mail matter in the dead letter office, are there any registered letters?
I believe so. But most are parcels and articles-an enormous amount, of course.
Has the minister given any attention to this matter of rural mail delivery?

Oh, yes. The hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) has given it more attention, perhaps, at least in this House, but I have also given some attention to it. I do not suppose that, at this hour, the hon. member (Mr. Fowler) would ask me to repeat the arguments I advanced, not against rural mail delivery, but against the expediency of our adopting it now. I would rather refer my hon. friend to the speech I delivered on the same subject in this House not very long ago. Briefly, the United States have adopted this system; but they have a population of 85,000.000 and an enormous postal revenue, w7ith a territory no larger and a climiate more favourable for this purpose than ours.
How does the minister establish that? We can drive sleighs in the w'inter time.
Yes. but we have the Yukon; we have the Labrador coast.
They have Alaska.
Yes, but we have many distant districts.
We have the islands that Captain Bernier has taken possession of.

Yes, where there are splendid deposits of coal which it is important for us to secure. We have a postal revenue that is buoyant and a fiair surplus, but we have not the postal resources of the United States. But, I would rather not excite my hon. friend from East Lambton on this subject at this moment. The question is an open question, and later on we will discuss it.
I was only anxious to know whether the minister was seriously considering it.
I am seriously considering it and it is a very interesting question.

In the contracts with the railway companies for carrying the mails, what power is reserved to the department . in case the service is not carried out? Last winter there was a railway in the county 1 have the honour to represent that, for two weeks, had not a train run on it. It became so serious that people there had to go many miles in order to get provisions. I brought the matter before the Railway Commission and it was attended to almost immediately. In the first instance, i thought of going to the Post Office Department about it. to learn whether the Postmaster General had any power in such a case.

Yes. No service, no pay. But, of course, the people prefer to have the service than to have the payment kept back ; and in such cases I always advise them to apply to the Railway Commission to have the service carried out.

Do I understand that the department has no power to inflict a penalty upon a railway company in such a case other than to withhold play for the exact time during which they have not rendered the service ?
That is the penalty.
Has the hon. minister a surplus, and, if so, of what amount ?

The surplus will be in the neighbourhood of $1,500,000 and $1,600,-
000.
What does the minister propose to do with it ?
Spend It in the best interests of the postal service-but cautiously.

The minister seems to be spending it very cautiously. I hope he does not intend to hand it over to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). That hon. gentleman will get rid of it Mr. FOSTER.
quickly enough. It would be better to spend a portion of it in improving the postal service which certainly needs improvement.

I am doing my best. I do not think there is an hon. member of this House who can say that he has come to the Postmaster General with a fair request and been refused. I have multiplied the services wherever it could fairly be said thiat they were not sufficient to keep up with the increase of population and in accordance with the good times that have prevailed. Where there were tri-weekly services I have established daily services ; where there were daily services I have established semi-daily services. I have reduced the distance between post offices. Formerly we did not establish post offices in ordiniarily thickly-settled parts of- the country at distances of much less than from six to eight miles. Now we have post offices four miles, or three, or even two miles apart. Where there is a mill, a school, a church or an establishment of any consequence, we never say no to the request for a post office.
Has the minister withdrawn the postal service on the river boats that run between St. John and Fredericton?
No.
I understood he had.

Last year, there was, I would not like to say a hold-up, but some thing very like a hold-up at the oirening of the season. They said they would not carry the mails unless we would double the subsidy to something like that. Then, we had to protect ourselves. This season it is all arranged, and we will carry the mails as before.
I was surprised to hear the Postmaster General state that he had tried to establish post offices at distances of four and five miles.
Two miles.
Iu thickly-settled sections.

In our country, even in what we call thickly-settled portions-where we have a settler on every section, or, possibly, every quarter-section-there are people who have to drive fifteen miles for their mail. It is quite common to go seven or eight miles. I speak of only one particular section, but I think this is fairly general.

If the hon. gentleman would point out to me a section of 25 to 30 people I would certainly establish a post office. That is my policy. Of course, we cannot have a post office at every door; but if there is any considerable number of people gathered, we establish a post office. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Herron) will

look at the postal map of his section, he will see that the post offices are there. It is not the same in the west as in the east, which is much more densely populated.

The minister has stated that by reducing the rate in the cities from two cents to one cent, lie will increase the revenue to the department. Now there is still a million and a half of money to be spent in the rural districts in a year, that is the department is bringing in a million and a half more money than they are going to make use of.

I do not say a million and a half more. I say that the reduction of postage from 2 cents to 1 cent for drop letters will increase the revenue. But the hon. gentleman should not lose sight of the fact that the cities are paying for the deficiencies of the rural districts. Toronto, Hamilton, London, Brantford, Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, Winnipeg especially, are paying for the service in the rural districts. When my Bill comes up I will establish these facts by figures.

I will have to see the figures before I accept that statement. I feel that the minister has not given the subject quite as much attention as he ought to. In the United States they are expending this year $36,000,000 on a rural free delivery service for about 18,000,000 people, that is practically $2 to each person. Now if the minister will investigate the conditions in the province of Ontario, he will find that we have about 40,000 square miles of territory that can be covered with a rural free mail delivery, covered successfully ; and in the province of Quebec about 20,000 square miles. When the minister states that because the United States has 80,000,000 of a population Canada must wait until we have 20,000,000, I am satisfied that he does not understand the question.

The hon. gentleman forgets that the United States did not establish that system when they had 00,000,000 people, or even when they had 70,000,000 ; they had nearly 80,000,000 when they started rural mail delivery. The system has been in existence in England for nearly a century, it has been in existence in France, Switzerland and some portions of Germany for years and years. But there is no comparison with the conditions in those thickly settled countries and the conditions prevailing in much the greater portion of Canada. Why, you could put England in Lake Superior and you would not see the shores of England. Of course, I admit that in some portions of Ontario the system might be established. I do not know of any more prosperous section of the British empire than the province of Ontario, there is no more intelligent portion of the British empire 290
than the province of Ontario. But if you give free rural mail delivery to one section of the country why should you not extend it to another? My hon. friend speaks of Lambton, of the Niagara peninsula, of the county of Essex, and that beautiful section of Ontario, and he says that surely they are entitled to free rural mail delivery. But what about Gaspe, what about Kings and Albert, what about Argenteuil, what about Carleton ?
Does the minister mean to suggest that there is any more prosperous section of Ontario than the county of Carleton ?
Surely not from an intellectual point of view.

We could establish free rural delivery in a large portion of Ontario, Quebec, the eastern provinces and some parts of the western provinces. But the minister intimates that all those districts must wait until the rest of the country is filled up. until Gaspe, or Argenteuil, or some of those outlying districts are filled up. If that is the position the minister takes with regard to rural delivery, I see very little hope for it.

I have a standing invitation from the hon. gentleman to discuss that question before the farmers of Lamb-ton. I would like to explain to the farmers of Lambton that their member in the House has made very nice and very able speeches in favour of rural mail delivery, that he was quite ready to spend in Canada what the United States are spending, and when his electors from Lambton learn that it will cost millions and millions beyond the revenue we have, they will probably give a cold douche to my hon. friend and his proposal will have to wait for a few years.
The minister is not fairly stating the question when he says that we will have to spend millions in Canada to establish this service in the thickly settled portions of the different provinces.
I do not want to establish it in any portion but I want to give it to the whole country.

The minister knows that in the United States no route can be established unless there are 100 families^ on that route. A standard route is 24 miles long and in the outlying districts of the United States they are not being served by a rural free mail delivery at all. The minister talks about it costing millions and millions to serve the people in Canada.
$29,000,000 in the United States.
I am aware of it. I say that it cost $36,000,000. But, they are serving nearly 20 million people.
They are discriminating.

I would ask the minister if in the thinly settled portions of the country they say that the farmers in the thickly settled portions are discriminating against them. As far as rural mail delivery is concerned we cannot have it if the present position of the minister is maintained. He may talk about the population of the United States and about their not having adopted it until they had 80 millions people. It is folly to approach the subject in that way. He might as well say that the telephone and telegraphs and all new inventions for the dissemination of knowledge throughout the country should not be made available to the people.
You require a city of a certain size, do you not, before you give free mail delivery ?
Yes, the new regulation requires a population of 12,000 and a revenue of $20,000.
Does the minister consider that cities just a little under that are discriminated against ?
Well, we apply good common sense to it.

Of course you do. What is the difference between that principle and the principle of establishing routes wherever there are a certain number of persons? That is exactly the principle the minister carries out with regard to cities and towns.

I would suggest that an experiment be made of the rural mail delivery system in Kings and Albert, and if it is satisfactory there and not too expensive the minister might apply it to outlying districts such as Lambton and others like that.

I would like to ask the minister if, in his annual balance sheet, he charges up anything against the postal revenue for the money invested in buildings put up for the purpose of carrying on the post office work. Does he not think there should be a certain proportion charged against this money which is invested purely for the carrying on of the work of the department ?
Not always, public buildings very frequently include the customs and the public works as well as the post office.

I know, but a good many of these buildings are put up for carrying on the postal work of the country. A portion of the cost of those buildings should be charged against the department so that the people would have an opportunity of seeing just how our postal matters stand. I would like to ask the minister if the Post Office Department is
required to approve of the erection of new buildings before the work is begun ?

Yes, when the erection of a public building is proposed the Department of Public Works receives, through my department, a statement of the revenue, the population, the postal facilities required and the probable revenue for the future. We generally say if a public building should be erected or not. We are the determining voice, generally speaking.
Why do you put up post office buildings in places with a small population and leave large towns without public buildings ?
There does not seem to-be a quorum present. The committee had better rise under those circumstances.
Do you not thiuk we should carry this item. I have given all the explanations.
I would not have any objection to this passing.

I will give the explanation with reference to the mail service.
There is an increase of $93,500 made up as follows :	*
Ordinary land service	$53,500-
Mail service by railways	 10,000
Mail service by steamboats	 20,000
Supply and repair of mail bags.. ..	10,000
The vote for land service is for new post offices, increase in the frequency of existing services, increased price of old contracts renewed, and submitted to public tender. The increase for the mail service by railways is chiefly to provide for the extension of the service in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. The miscellaneous is as follows : Travelling charges, $3,000, stationery, printing, advertising, $5,000, postage stamps, post cards envelopes $10,000, other miscellaneous items, $42,000.
Your postage stamps are by contract ?	'
Yes.
This miscellaneous vote includes the payment of labourers ?
Yes, we have to employ extra men at busy seasons.
Who employs the labourers in Montreal, for instance ?

The postmaster.
Mr. FOSTER, Has he sole authority ?
They are appointed under my authority. He writes to the department that he requires 20 men say for such a time and I have a list of names that are sent to me.
By whom?

I may say they are sent by members of parliament on both sides of the House and by others. There are applications coming in all the time by the hundreds. If the postmaster at Montreal or Toronto asks for twenty men I send him a list of 50 or 60 names and the applicants are brought before them and tested. I have given the assistant-postmaster at Montreal complete discretion as to the selection of the men. My hon. friend will understand it would be very risky to take men for post office work simply because they are recommended by politicians, and we must find out if they are reliable and trustworthy.
What test is made?
He sends for their parents or their friends and asks for certificates and when they are well recommended he appoints them.
Does he make any test as to their mental qualifications?

When they are merely to do labouring work such as carrying mail bags they do not require much education but sometimes they enter as labourers and they are employed in the sorting of letters and so on. Of course you will not find university graduates or men who have passed the civil service examination who will take $1.25 or up to $2 a day.

The minister of course has followed precedent, but I would suggest that in future these estimates should be given in more detail so that we will not have an appropriation of $504,000 under the head of miscellaneous, and which money could be devoted to any one of numerous subjects. Some of the departments bring down their estimates in the greatest detail and others bring them down in three or four huge items at the tail end of which is a miscellaneous vote which can be utilized for any possible purpose. That is not according to the spirit of parliamentary control over government expenditure.

I admit there is room for improvement there and will try in the future to have more detail.
